subject: rla
title: Comparing Two Texts on the Same Topic
objectives: You will identify the central idea or claim and the purpose of each passage in a pair.
You will compare two authors' points of view, including who is speaking, what each believes, and what each has at stake.
You will compare the kinds and quality of evidence two authors use to support their ideas.
You will synthesize two texts by deciding where they agree, disagree, add to each other, or complicate each other.
You will answer paired-passage questions in GED formats, including “both passages,” “one passage only,” and “how does Passage 2 relate to Passage 1.”

slides.title: Comparing Two Texts on the Same Topic
slides.board:
Week 6 · Reasoning Through Language Arts

Today you will:

  • Label each passage: who, main point, purpose
  • Compare two points of view
  • Judge whose evidence is stronger
  • Synthesize: agree, disagree, add, complicate
  • Answer “both passages” and “one passage only” questions

Plan: Warm-up · Learn and practice together · Your turn · GED questions · Recap

notes.say: Welcome to week 6. Until now we have read one text at a time. Today the GED hands you two texts on the same topic and asks how they connect: what they share, how their purposes and points of view differ, and whose evidence is stronger. This is also the exact thinking behind the extended response in weeks 9 and 10, where you read two arguments and decide which one is better supported. Everything you learn today, you will use again on the essay.
ask: Think of a time two people told you different versions of the same event. How did you decide whom to believe? (expected: any honest answer; listen for “I thought about what each person had at stake” or “I checked the facts” and build on it)

slides.title: Warm-up: last week's argument skills
slides.board:
(1) Our town should build a covered skate park. (2) Last year, police wrote 63 tickets for skating in downtown parking lots. (3) A covered park would give skaters a legal place to go all year. (4) Some say the park would cost too much, (5) but a state recreation grant would pay for half.

  1. Which sentence is the claim?
  2. Which sentence is evidence (a fact)?
  3. Which sentence is a reason?
  4. Find the counterclaim and the rebuttal.
steps: 1. Sentence 1 is the claim: what the writer wants us to believe or do.
2. Sentence 2 is evidence: a specific number (63 tickets).
3. Sentence 3 is a reason: why the writer thinks the park is a good idea.
4. Counterclaim: part 4, “Some say the park would cost too much.” Rebuttal: part 5, “a state recreation grant would pay for half.”

notes.say: This warm-up reviews week 5: the parts of an argument. Give the student about two minutes, then take the answers one at a time. Today we will look for these same parts in two texts at once, so a quick, confident answer here is a good sign. If the student hesitates on the counterclaim, remind them that it is the other side's view, usually introduced by “Some say” or “Critics argue.”
notes.answer: 1. Sentence 1. 2. Sentence 2 (63 tickets). 3. Sentence 3. 4. Counterclaim: the park would cost too much. Rebuttal: a grant would pay for half.
notes.watch: Some students call sentence 2 the claim because it has a number. Ask: “Is the writer trying to convince you of the 63 tickets, or using them to prove something else?”

slides.title: Warm-up: spot the weak reasoning
slides.board:
Name the problem.

  1. “I wore my lucky socks, and our team won three straight games. The socks work.”
  2. “If we let students use phones at lunch, next they will use them in class, then during tests, and soon nobody will learn anything.”
  3. “Either we close the pool or the town goes broke.”
  4. Which is stronger evidence that buses run late? (a) a transit agency study of 12,000 trips (b) “My neighbor says the buses are always late.”
steps: 1. False cause. The wins came after the socks, but nothing shows the socks caused them.
2. Slippery slope. Each step is assumed, not proven.
3. Either-or. It pretends there are only two choices; the town could raise fees, cut hours, or find a grant.
4. (a), a large study from a named source. (b) is one secondhand report, and “always” claims more than it can prove.

notes.say: More week 5 review, aimed at faulty reasoning and evidence quality. Today the GED will ask “whose evidence is stronger?” across two passages, and the weak moves we named last week are exactly what make one passage weaker than the other. Ask the student to name each problem and say why it is a problem.
notes.answer: 1. False cause. 2. Slippery slope. 3. Either-or (false choice). 4. (a), the study of 12,000 trips; (b) is an anecdote with an overgeneralization (“always”).
notes.watch: If the student says (b) is stronger “because the neighbor rides the bus,” name the trap now: personal experience feels convincing, but one person cannot show what happens on 12,000 trips. We will meet this trap all day.

slides.title: Two texts, one topic: the routine
slides.board:
Paired passages are two texts on the same topic, usually by different writers with different reasons for writing.

  1. Read Passage 1 alone. Label it: Who? Main point? Why written?
  2. Read Passage 2 alone. Label it the same way.
  3. Compare on four points: claim · purpose · point of view · evidence.
  4. Synthesize: Agree · Disagree · Add · Complicate.
  5. Answer. For “both” questions, check both passages.

notes.say: Here is the whole lesson on one slide. The biggest mistake on paired passages is trying to compare while still reading the first text; students end up giving one author credit for the other author's idea. So we read each passage alone and write a short label, just three things: who is writing, what their main point is, and why they wrote it. A label takes thirty seconds and saves several wrong answers. Model one now: “P1: reporter, city may lower speed limit, inform.”
ask: Why read each passage alone before comparing? (expected: so you know each author's point and purpose and don't mix up who said what)
What three things go in a label? (expected: who is writing, the main point, the purpose)
notes.watch: Students often skip the label because it feels slow. Time it: thirty seconds per passage. Then show how one label settles a question instantly.

slides.title: Purpose: genre and language clues
slides.board:
PurposeCommon genresLanguage clues
Informnews report, fact sheet, textbookthird person, numbers, several views
Explainhow-to, science or history articlebecause, as a result, steps
Persuadeeditorial, letter, speech, adshould, must, strong words, call to action
Narrate or reflectmemoir, diary, story“I,” scenes, feelings

Check the ending: a request (“Vote no”) signals persuasion.

notes.say: The four purposes come from week 3, but on paired passages the purposes are often different from each other, and the GED asks about that difference directly. The genre is your first clue; a fact sheet from the county almost always informs, a letter to the editor almost always persuades. The language is your second clue. And the ending is your tiebreaker: a writer who wants something from you usually asks for it in the last paragraph.
ask: A blog post ends, “Come see the difference for yourself next fall.” What purpose does that ending suggest? (expected: persuade; it is an invitation, a call to action)
notes.watch: A text can inform and still lean toward a side. If a news report quotes a supporter, the report is still informing. Save “persuade” for texts where the writer states a position or asks for action.

slides.title: Compare purpose: the Mill Creek Dam
slides.board:
Text A (county fact sheet): The Mill Creek Dam was built in 1911 to power a sawmill that closed in 1958. Removing it next summer will cost an estimated $2.1 million; repairing its cracked spillway would cost $3.4 million. Removal will reopen about 12 miles of creek to migrating fish.

Text B (fishing guide's blog): I've guided trips on Mill Creek for twenty years, and that dam is a wall across the best water in the county. Taking it out is the best news this creek has had in a century. Come see the difference next fall.

How do the purposes differ?
steps: Label A: county · dam removal, its cost and results · inform (dates, costs, neutral voice).
Label B: fishing guide · removal is great news · express support and persuade (“I,” “best news,” an invitation).
Compare: A states no opinion, though its numbers make removal look sensible. B is first person from someone with a stake: he guides trips on the creek.
Answer: Text A informs readers about the plan and its costs; Text B shares an enthusiastic personal view to win support for removal.

notes.say: Model the routine out loud. Label each text first, then compare. Point out that the two texts end up on the same side of the issue, but for different reasons and with different purposes. Same topic, same conclusion, different jobs.
ask: Do the two texts agree or disagree about removing the dam? (expected: they agree; A's numbers favor removal, B celebrates it)

slides.title: Together: same event, two voices
slides.board:
Text A (museum announcement): Starting in May, the Lakeview History Museum will offer free admission on the first Sunday of every month. The program is funded by a community grant. Regular admission is $14 for adults.

Text B (visitor review): We went on the first free Sunday, and it was packed. My kids loved the old fire engine, but we waited forty minutes just to get in. Free is nice. Next time I'd rather pay the $14 and actually see things.

  1. What fact appears in both?
  2. What is each text's purpose?
  3. Does the writer of B think the program is a good idea?
steps: 1. Both: free admission on the first Sunday, and regular admission is $14.
2. A informs readers about a new program. B shares a personal experience and an opinion.
3. Mixed. B likes the exhibits and says “Free is nice,” but would rather pay to avoid the crowd.

notes.say: Now the student leads and you guide. Have them label each text out loud before answering. Reveal each step only after the student answers it. Question 3 is the important one: it has no one-word answer.
ask: What words in B show mixed feelings? (expected: “Free is nice” versus “I'd rather pay the $14”)
notes.answer: 1. Free first Sundays; regular admission is $14. 2. A informs; B shares an experience and an opinion. 3. Mixed: B values free admission and the exhibits but dislikes the crowds and would pay to avoid them.
notes.watch: Students want a clean yes or no on question 3. Paired-passage questions often reward the reader who notices partial agreement. Ask, “What does B like? What does B dislike?”

slides.title: Point of view: who, what, what's at stake
slides.board:
1. Who is speaking? Reporter, expert, worker, family member? First person (“I”) or third person? Insider or outsider?
  2. What does the speaker believe about the topic?
  3. What is at stake for the speaker?

Reporting a view is not holding it. A news story that quotes a farmer who opposes a highway does not itself oppose the highway.

A stake shapes what a writer notices. It does not make the writer wrong.

notes.say: Point of view has two parts: who is talking and what they believe. On paired passages I add a third question: what does this person have at stake? A delivery driver writing about speed limits has a personal interest. That does not make him wrong, but it shapes what he notices and what he leaves out. The other big idea: a neutral report can quote people on both sides without taking a side itself. Quoting is not agreeing.
ask: A reporter quotes a parent who wants the school kept open. Does the reporter want the school kept open? (expected: not necessarily; reporting a view is not holding it)
Does having a stake mean a writer is wrong? (expected: no; it means we check the evidence carefully)
notes.watch: Watch for students who dismiss any writer with a stake (“he just wants money”). That is last week's attack-on-the-person error. Judge the evidence, not the person.

slides.title: Compare points of view: the bypass
slides.board:
Text A (news report): The state plans a two-lane bypass around Carver to move trucks off Main Street. Planners estimate it would cut downtown truck traffic by about 60 percent. “It would split my farm in half,” said Ruth Ambrose, whose family has farmed east of town since 1938.

Text B (letter by Ruth Ambrose): The bypass would leave my cattle on one side of a highway and my barn on the other. Main Street's truck traffic is a real problem. But there is an old rail line north of town the state never studied. Study it before you take my land.

Compare the points of view.
steps: Who: A is a reporter, third person, an outsider. B is a farmer, first person, an insider whose land is on the route.
Beliefs: A states no opinion; it reports the plan and quotes Ambrose. B opposes the route but admits the truck traffic is real.
Stake: B could lose her farmland. That explains her focus, but her rail-line idea is still an argument we can check.
Answer: A reports the plan from the outside without taking a side; B, directly affected, accepts the problem but opposes this route and proposes another.

notes.say: Walk through the three point-of-view questions for each text. The trap here is that Ambrose's quote appears inside Text A, so careless readers say Text A opposes the bypass. Show that Text A reports the plan, the planners' numbers, and one opponent; it never states a view of its own.
ask: Does Ambrose disagree with everything in Text A? (expected: no; she agrees the truck traffic is a problem)

slides.title: Together: the scooter program
slides.board:
Passage 1 (city report): In its first year, the Eastport scooter-share program recorded 212,000 rides. A rider survey found that 31 percent of trips replaced a car trip. The city received 640 complaints, most about scooters left on sidewalks. Next year, riders who park outside a marked zone will pay a $10 fee.

Passage 2 (letter): I use a wheelchair, and twice this month a scooter lying across the Bay Street sidewalk forced me to turn around. The city says the program takes cars off the road, and maybe it does. But a $10 fee will not fix this. Require racks, or end the program.

  1. Purpose of each?
  2. One fact in both?
  3. How does P2 relate to the 640 complaints?
  4. Does P2 reject everything in P1?
steps: 1. P1 informs about first-year results and a new rule. P2 persuades the city to act more strongly.
2. The $10 fee; scooters left on sidewalks; the claim that the program reduces car trips (P2 grants “maybe it does”).
3. P2 adds a personal example of the sidewalk problem and complicates the report: for some people the problem is serious, not minor.
4. No. The writer accepts that the program may reduce car trips but says the fee is not enough.

notes.say: Have the student label both passages first: who, point, purpose. Then work the four questions. Question 3 previews synthesis: the letter turns a statistic into a real person's experience, and shows that the problem is bigger for some people than a number suggests.
ask: Who is speaking in Passage 2, and what is at stake for her? (expected: a wheelchair user; her ability to use the sidewalk)
notes.answer: 1. P1 informs; P2 persuades. 2. The $10 fee, or scooters on sidewalks, or fewer car trips. 3. It adds a personal case and complicates the report by showing the problem is serious for some people. 4. No; the writer concedes the program may reduce car trips.
notes.watch: If the student says the two passages “totally disagree,” point to “maybe it does.” Writers on opposite sides often share facts.

slides.title: History and memoir: the Erie Canal
slides.board:
Text A (textbook): The Erie Canal opened in 1825. It linked the Hudson River to Lake Erie and cut the cost of shipping goods between New York City and the Great Lakes region. Towns along its route grew quickly.

Text B (a canal worker's diary, written for this lesson): Walked the towpath twelve hours today behind the mules. My boots are through at the heel. Captain says we reach Buffalo by Thursday if the locks are clear.

How do purpose and point of view differ? What does B add?
steps: Label A: textbook writer, outside view, third person · the canal's importance · inform.
Label B: a worker, inside view, first person · one hard day on the canal · record personal experience.
Relationship: they do not disagree. B adds what the work felt like, which A never covers.
Answer: A explains why the canal mattered to a whole region; B shows one person's daily experience of working on it.

notes.say: The GED sometimes pairs an informational text with a literary one: a history and a memoir, an article and a diary. The questions are the same, but the answers often line up in a pattern: the history is general, third person, and informs; the personal text is specific, first person, and narrates or reflects. Make sure the student notices that Text B is a fictional diary written for this lesson.
ask: Could Text B be used to prove that the canal cut shipping costs? (expected: no; it is one worker's day and says nothing about costs)

slides.title: Comparing evidence
slides.board:
TypeStrong when…Weak when…
Statistics, datasource named; numbers fit the claimno source; stretched to prove more
Expert statementexpert works in that fieldno real connection to the topic
Anecdoteillustrates what other evidence showsone case used to prove something about everyone
Exampletypical and relevantrare or off topic

Red flags: everyone, always, nobody, never · no source · a prediction with no support

notes.say: Last week you judged evidence in one argument. Today you judge it in two and decide which writer's support is stronger. The key question is always: does this evidence prove the claim as stated, or only one case of it? A moving personal story can feel stronger than a statistic, but one story cannot tell you what happens across a whole city. Notice that I am not saying stories are worthless. A story that illustrates what the data already shows is useful; a story that replaces the data is weak.
ask: Name two signs that evidence might be weak. (expected: no source; one anecdote used for everyone; words like “everyone” or “always”; unsupported predictions)
notes.watch: Students tend to judge evidence by whether they agree with the writer. Ask them to judge it as if they held the opposite opinion.

slides.title: Whose evidence is stronger? Late fees
slides.board:
Text A (library director): Two years ago, the Pine Hollow Library stopped charging late fees. Since then, 1,140 cardholders whose accounts had been blocked for unpaid fines have returned to borrowing. The share of books returned within a month of the due date has stayed at about 96 percent.

Text B (resident's letter): Getting rid of late fees was a mistake. Everyone knows people only return things on time when there's a penalty. My neighbor kept a library book for half a year. Without fines, the shelves will be empty within a year.
steps: List A: two specific numbers from library records, measured over two years.
List B: “everyone knows” (no proof), one neighbor's story (an anecdote), and a prediction with no support.
Test: if fines were needed, the return rate should have fallen. It stayed at about 96 percent. A's data contradicts B's prediction.
Answer: Text A is better supported: specific, relevant data over time versus an unsupported generalization and one anecdote.

notes.say: List the evidence in each text before judging it. Then show the student the most powerful move in paired passages: one text's evidence can directly test the other text's claim. Text B predicts that returns will collapse; Text A has two years of data showing they did not.
ask: Text A comes from the library director, who has a reason to defend the policy. Does that cancel the data? (expected: no; it is worth noticing, but the numbers are specific and checkable)

slides.title: Together: self-checkout
slides.board:
Text A (grocery chain announcement): Since adding self-checkout lanes at its twelve stores last year, Fresh Way has cut average checkout wait times from 7 minutes to 4 minutes, according to its store records.

Text B (letter from a cashier): Self-checkout is a disaster. Customers hate it. Yesterday a man spent ten minutes fighting with a machine that would not read his coupons.

  1. What kind of evidence does each text use?
  2. Which gives stronger support for its claim?
  3. What should a careful reader notice about who wrote Text A?
steps: 1. A: data from store records across twelve stores over a year. B: “Customers hate it” (a generalization with no proof) and one customer's story.
2. Text A. One slow customer cannot show what happens to most customers.
3. A comes from the company, which wants to look good. That is a reason to check it, but its claim is still specific and measurable.

notes.say: Let the student list the evidence and decide. Push for a reason, not just a pick. Question 3 is about bias: the company has a reason to look good. A careful reader notes that, then still asks whether the claim is specific and checkable.
ask: What would make Text B's claim stronger? (expected: a customer survey, complaint counts, or wait-time data)
notes.answer: 1. A uses records-based data; B uses an unsupported generalization and one anecdote. 2. Text A. 3. It may be biased toward its own program, so it deserves a second look, but its evidence is specific and checkable.
notes.watch: Some students choose B because the cashier “is there every day.” Ask: “Does being there every day let her count the wait times at twelve stores?”

slides.title: Synthesize with ADAC
slides.board:
To synthesize is to combine two sources into a fuller understanding. Two texts can relate in four ways:

AgreeBoth support the same point.
DisagreeThey make opposite claims.
AddOne gives new information that fits the other.
ComplicateOne shows the other's point is not the whole story: a limit, an exception, or a cost.

Pairs often do more than one: agree on a fact, complicate the conclusion.

notes.say: ADAC is the heart of today. When a GED question asks how Passage 2 relates to Passage 1, name the relationship first, then look for the answer that matches. The tricky pair is add versus complicate. Add means new information that fits; nothing about the first text's point changes. Complicate means the new information makes the first text's point less simple: it shows a limit, an exception, or a cost. And many real pairs do both: they agree on the facts and complicate the conclusion.
ask: What is the difference between add and complicate? (expected: add is new, compatible information; complicate shows a limit, exception, or cost that makes the first point less simple)
notes.watch: Students over-use “disagree.” Before accepting it, ask: “Do they make opposite claims, or does one just point out a problem?”

slides.title: Synthesis: the four-day week
slides.board:
Text A (company report): During a six-month trial, Harlan Logistics moved its office staff to a four-day, 36-hour week with no cut in pay. Sick days fell 22 percent, and the number of employees who quit dropped from 14 to 5.

Text B (warehouse supervisor): The four-day week has been great for the office, and I'm happy for them. But my team runs the loading dock, and trucks arrive six days a week. If the company keeps this program, it needs a plan for workers whose jobs don't fit a four-day schedule.

Which statement do both support? (a) End the four-day week. (b) It has worked well for office staff. (c) Every employee should move to it. (d) Warehouse workers quit more often.
steps: (a) Neither text says to end it. Out.
(b) A's data shows it worked for office staff; B says “great for the office.” Both support it.
(c) B says the dock cannot fit a four-day schedule, so B rejects this. Out.
(d) Neither text compares quit rates by job. Out. Answer: (b). B agrees about the office and complicates the report with a limit.

notes.say: Test every choice against both texts, out loud. Then name the relationship. Text B agrees about the office and complicates the report by pointing out workers it does not cover. That is the agree-and-complicate pattern you will see again and again.
ask: Is Text B against the four-day week? (expected: no; B is happy for the office and asks for a plan for other workers)

slides.title: Together: name the relationship
slides.board:
Is Text B agreeing, disagreeing, adding, or complicating?

  1. A: “The new clinic hours have made it easier for working families to see a doctor.” B: “The 7 a.m. opening is a real help for families like mine who work days.”
  2. A: “The new bike lanes have made Elm Avenue safer for cyclists.” B: “Bike crashes on Elm are down, but delivery trucks now double-park in the lane every morning, pushing riders into traffic.”
  3. A: “Recycling has cut the trash sent to the landfill.” B: “Recycling has not cut landfill trash; the totals have stayed the same for three years.”
  4. A: “The Oak Street bridge closes June 1 for repairs.” B: “The bridge closes June 1, and crews expect to reopen it by mid-August.”
steps: 1. Agree. Both say the new hours help working families.
2. Complicate. B accepts that crashes are down but shows a new danger, a limit on “safer.”
3. Disagree. Opposite claims about landfill trash.
4. Add. B confirms the date and adds when the bridge should reopen; nothing in A is challenged or limited.

notes.say: Have the student name the relationship for each pair and give a reason before you reveal it. If they hesitate between add and complicate on number 2, ask whether B's information changes how simple A's point is. If they hesitate on number 4, ask whether B's reopening date makes A's statement less true.
notes.watch: Number 2 is the one students miss: they see “crashes are down” and say “agree.” Ask, “Does B think the lane is simply safer now?” B accepts the good news but shows a new danger, so it complicates. On number 4, a student may say “agree”; point out that B goes beyond A with a new fact, the reopening date.

slides.title: Three paired-passage questions
slides.board:
QuestionHow to answer
“Supported by both passages”Two-check rule: point to a line in P1 and a line in P2.
“In Passage 1 but not Passage 2”Find it in P1, then search P2 to rule it out.
“How does Passage 2 relate to Passage 1?”Name the ADAC relationship first, then match.

The trap: a choice that is true, but for only one passage.

notes.say: These three question types cover most paired-passage items on the GED. The most common wrong answer on a “both” question is a choice that is true for one passage. It feels right because it is in the text. The two-check rule beats it: you must be able to put a finger on a line in Passage 1 and a line in Passage 2. If you can only find one, cross it out. For “not mentioned” questions, do the reverse: find it in one passage, then hunt for it in the other.
ask: A choice is true according to Passage 2 but never mentioned in Passage 1. Can it answer a “both” question? (expected: no; it fails the two-check rule)
notes.watch: On drag-and-drop versions (“Passage 1 only / Passage 2 only / Both”), students rush the Both bin. Make them do the two-check for every card.

slides.title: The two-check rule in action
slides.board:
Text A (shelter flyer): Adopting an adult dog from Riverbend Animal Shelter costs $75 and includes vaccines and a microchip. Adult dogs are often already house-trained.

Text B (veterinarian's column): Shelter dogs can make wonderful pets, and adult dogs are often calmer than puppies. Still, plan for costs after adoption: food, checkups, and supplies usually add several hundred dollars in the first year.

Which do both texts support? (a) Adult shelter dogs can be good pets. (b) A dog's first-year cost is $75. (c) Puppies make better pets. (d) Adult dogs are calmer than puppies.
steps: (a) A: house-trained adult dogs. B: “can make wonderful pets.” Both.
(b) $75 is only the adoption fee; B says first-year costs are several hundred dollars. B complicates A here.
(c) B says the opposite: adult dogs are often calmer. Out.
(d) True in B, but A never mentions calmness. B only. Answer: (a).

notes.say: Run the two-check rule on every choice, out loud: “Where is it in A? Where is it in B?” Choice (d) is the best teaching moment: it is true according to B, and students pick it for that reason, but A never compares adult dogs with puppies.
ask: What is the relationship between the texts on cost? (expected: B complicates A; the $75 fee is not the whole cost)

slides.title: Your turn: purpose and point of view
slides.board:
Text A (power company notice): Crews will replace utility poles on Ridge Road from May 4 to May 8. Expect lane closures from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m.

Text B (neighborhood post): Ridge Road closures again! Last time the “five-day” job took two weeks and I was late to my shift every day. Leave early, neighbors.

  1. What is the purpose of each text?
  2. Who is speaking in B, and what is at stake for that person?
  3. A news story quotes a parent who wants Lincoln School kept open. Does the story want the school kept open?
steps: 1. A informs (dates, hours, neutral). B warns and advises neighbors, sharing a personal complaint.
2. A resident, first person, who commutes on Ridge Road. At stake: getting to work on time.
3. Not necessarily. Reporting a view is not holding it; check whether the story presents other views and states its own.

notes.say: Start a three-minute timer and stay quiet while the student works. When time is up, have the student give each answer with a reason before you reveal anything.
notes.answer: 1. A informs; B shares an experience to warn and advise neighbors (persuade them to leave early). 2. A resident who drives Ridge Road to work; being late to work. 3. No; quoting a parent does not mean the story takes the parent's side.
notes.watch: If the student says B's purpose is “to inform,” ask what B wants readers to do. The last line is an instruction: “Leave early.”

slides.title: Your turn: evidence
slides.board:
1. P1: “According to the county health department, flu cases among children fell 28 percent in the two years after the school vaccine clinics began.” P2: “Those clinics don't work. My daughter got the shot and still caught the flu.” Which is stronger evidence, and why?
  2. Name the weakness: “Everyone on my block says the new trash pickup is worse.”
  3. A passage's numbers come from the company that runs the program it describes. Does that make them worthless?
steps: 1. P1. A specific number from a named source over two years. P2 is one case; one child catching the flu cannot show what happened to all children.
2. An unsupported generalization (“everyone”) based on neighbors' opinions, with no data.
3. No. Note the possible bias, then check whether the claim is specific, measurable, and from records that could be checked.

notes.say: Three minutes on the clock. This slide checks whether the student can explain why evidence is strong or weak, not just pick a side. Ask for the reason every time.
notes.answer: 1. P1: sourced data across many children versus a single anecdote. 2. Overgeneralization with no evidence (“everyone on my block”). 3. No; possible bias is a reason to look carefully, not to throw out specific, checkable data.
notes.watch: On question 1, a student may say P2 is “proof the shot doesn't work.” Ask: “If cases fell 28 percent, could some children still catch the flu?” Yes; fewer is not zero.

slides.title: Your turn: relationships and “both”
slides.board:
P1 (city report): The Oak Street farmers market drew 41,000 visits this season, up from 29,000 last year. Vendors accepted SNAP food benefits for the first time.

P2 (vendor's letter): This was my best season in eight years at Oak Street, and SNAP shoppers were a big part of it. But the market still has no shade or water for vendors, and two of us got heat sickness in July.

  1. Which is supported by both? (a) The market had a successful season. (b) SNAP was accepted for the first time. (c) Two vendors got heat sickness. (d) The market should close in July.
  2. Name the relationship of P2 to P1.
  3. Name one detail in P1 only.
steps: 1. (a). P1: visits rose from 29,000 to 41,000. P2: “my best season in eight years.” (b) “first time” is in P1 only; (c) is P2 only; (d) is in neither.
2. Agrees and complicates: P2 confirms a good season but shows a cost the report leaves out, vendor safety in the heat.
3. The visit numbers (41,000 and 29,000), or that SNAP was accepted for the first time.

notes.say: Three minutes. Insist on the two-check rule for question 1: the student should point to the line in each passage. For question 2, accept “agree and complicate” and ask for the part that agrees and the part that complicates.
notes.answer: 1. (a). 2. Agree and complicate (a successful season, but no shade or water and heat sickness). 3. Visit totals, or “for the first time.”
notes.watch: Choice (b) traps students because P2 mentions SNAP shoppers. Ask: “Does P2 say it was the first time?” It does not.

slides.title: GED question: supported by both
slides.board:
Passage 1: Since Lake City added a second ambulance crew in March, average response time fell from 11 minutes to 8, according to the fire department.

Passage 2 (paramedic's letter): The second crew has helped, and our times are better. But we are working 60-hour weeks to staff it. Without more hires, burnout will undo the gains.

Which statement is supported by both passages?

A. Response times improved after the second crew was added.
B. Paramedics are working 60-hour weeks.
C. The city should hire more paramedics right away.
D. Response times fell because paramedics worked longer hours.
steps: B is Passage 2 only: Passage 1 says nothing about hours worked.
C is Passage 2 only, and only implied: Passage 1 makes no recommendation.
D is not stated in either: neither passage says the longer hours caused the faster times. It twists two facts into a cause.
A is correct: Passage 1 gives 11 to 8 minutes; Passage 2 says “our times are better.”

notes.say: Treat this like the real test. Have the student label both passages, then run the two-check rule on each choice. Eliminate together and name the reason each time.
ask: Before you look at the choices, what do both writers agree on? (expected: the second crew made response times better)
notes.answer: A. B and C are Passage 2 only; D invents a cause neither passage states.

slides.title: GED question: how the texts relate
slides.board:
Passage 1 (fact sheet): Rain gardens are shallow planted beds that collect runoff from roofs and driveways. In a three-year study, the city found that rain gardens absorbed about 30 percent of runoff from nearby roofs. Each costs about $400.

Passage 2 (homeowner): We put in a rain garden two years ago, and our basement hasn't flooded since. Fair warning: it needed watering every other day the first summer, and weeding is weekly.

How does Passage 2 relate to Passage 1?

A. It contradicts Passage 1 by showing rain gardens do not reduce runoff.
B. It supports Passage 1's point that rain gardens help with runoff and adds the upkeep they need.
C. It repeats the city's study with the homeowner's own measurements.
D. It argues that rain gardens cost more to install than Passage 1 says.
steps: A is the opposite: the basement has not flooded since, which fits the study.
C is not stated: the homeowner gives no measurements, only an experience.
D is not stated: Passage 2 never mentions installation cost; upkeep is work, not a price.
B is correct: it agrees that rain gardens help and adds the watering and weeding Passage 1 never mentions.

notes.say: Name the relationship before reading the choices: the homeowner's experience fits the fact sheet (agree) and brings up something the fact sheet leaves out (add). Then eliminate.
ask: Is watering and weeding a reason to say Passage 2 disagrees? (expected: no; the homeowner still had good results and is warning readers about the work)
notes.answer: B. A reverses the homeowner's point; C invents measurements; D confuses upkeep with installation cost.
notes.watch: A sharp student may say the watering and weeding are a cost, so Passage 2 complicates Passage 1. That is a fair reading of the upkeep, but it does not undercut Passage 1's point that rain gardens absorb runoff; the homeowner's results confirm it. B is the only choice that fits both texts: it names the agreement and the new detail.

slides.title: GED question: history and memoir
slides.board:
Passage 1: Bookmobiles, libraries on wheels, carried books to rural areas that had no library building. They ran on regular schedules, stopping at schools, stores, and crossroads.

Passage 2 (memoir, written for this lesson): Every other Thursday the green truck stopped at Hadley's store, and I was always first in line. Mrs. Ochoa, the driver, knew I liked sea stories before I did. That truck is why I became a teacher.

Which best describes how the passages differ?

A. Passage 1 gives a general account of bookmobiles; Passage 2 tells how one bookmobile shaped the narrator's life.
B. Passage 1 argues that bookmobiles should return; Passage 2 argues they were not needed.
C. Passage 1 describes one driver's route; Passage 2 explains how bookmobiles began.
D. Passage 1 is told in first person; Passage 2 is told in third person.
steps: B is not stated: neither passage argues for or against bookmobiles.
C swaps the passages: the one driver and route are in Passage 2, and neither explains how bookmobiles began.
D swaps the points of view: Passage 2 uses “I”; Passage 1 is third person.
A is correct: general account versus one personal story.

notes.say: Label both: Passage 1 is general, third person, informing; Passage 2 is one person's memory, first person, reflecting. Then eliminate. Two of the wrong choices simply swap the passages, a very common GED distractor.
ask: What clue tells you Passage 2 is a memoir? (expected: first person “I,” a specific memory, reflection on what it meant)
notes.answer: A. B is not stated; C and D swap details between the passages.

slides.title: GED strategy: label before you answer
slides.board:
1. Thirty seconds per passage: on scratch paper, write “P1: who · point · purpose” and “P2: who · point · purpose.”
  2. Read the question and circle which passage it names: 1, 2, or both.
  3. One passage? Glance at its label, then go to the paragraph.
  4. Both? Two-check every choice.
  5. Relate? Name the ADAC relationship before reading the choices.

Most paired-passage misses come from giving one author the other author's idea. Labels prevent that.

notes.say: On the GED, paired passages appear as two texts on one screen, often with tabs. It is easy to lose track of which writer said what, especially when the two passages share facts. The labels act like name tags. They cost one minute and save points. Also, circling which passage the question names keeps the student from answering about the wrong text, which happens more than people think.
ask: Why circle which passage the question names? (expected: so you answer about the right text and know whether to two-check)

slides.title: Recap and next steps
slides.board:
• Read each passage alone. Label it: who · point · purpose.
  • Compare claim, purpose, point of view, evidence.
  • Reporting a view is not holding it. A stake shapes a view; it does not make it wrong.
  • Stronger evidence: specific, sourced, relevant. Weaker: “everyone,” one anecdote, no source.
  • Synthesize with ADAC. “Both” questions need the two-check rule.

Next: Student Lesson → Practice Set A (Set B if under 80%) → Exit Check

notes.say: Have the student say ADAC from memory and explain the two-check rule before you reveal the recap. Then walk through what comes next: the Student Lesson reviews today step by step with checks, Practice Set A has 15 GED-style questions on two pairs of passages with the reasoning behind every wrong answer, and the Exit Check confirms the skill. Remind them that weeks 9 and 10, the extended response, build directly on today.
ask: Which comparison is hardest for you: purpose, point of view, or evidence? (expected: any honest answer; suggest extra Student Lesson screens for that part)

screens.title: What you will learn
screens.html:
On the GED Reasoning Through Language Arts test, some reading sets give you two passages on the same topic. One might be a news article and the other a letter to the editor. One might be a history and the other a memoir. The questions ask how the two texts connect: what they share, how they differ, and which one makes a stronger case. It is also the main skill behind the extended response, so the time you spend here pays off twice. In this lesson you will learn to:

  • find the main point and purpose of each passage in a pair
  • compare two writers' points of view, including what each has at stake
  • compare the kind and quality of evidence each writer uses
  • synthesize: decide where two texts agree, disagree, add to each other, or complicate each other
  • answer “both passages,” “one passage only,” and “how does Passage 2 relate” questions

Work one screen at a time. Most screens end with a check question. You must answer it before you move on, and if you miss it, you will see exactly why that answer is wrong.

screens.title: Two texts, one topic: the routine
screens.html:
The biggest mistake on paired passages is trying to compare while you are still reading the first text. You end up giving one writer credit for the other writer's idea. Use this routine instead:

  1. Read Passage 1 alone. Write a short label: Who is writing? What is the main point? Why did they write it?
  2. Read Passage 2 alone. Label it the same way.
  3. Compare the two on four points: claim, purpose, point of view, and evidence.
  4. Synthesize: decide how the texts relate.
  5. Answer the questions, checking the passage each one names.

Label example: P1: reporter · city may lower the speed limit · inform. P2: delivery driver · fix dangerous streets instead · persuade.

check.prompt:
Complete the first rule of the routine with one word:

“Read each passage first. Then compare.”
check.hint: What should you not do while you are still reading the first passage?
check.explain: The first rule is to read each passage alone and label it (who, main point, purpose) before comparing. Comparing too early is how readers end up giving one writer the other writer's idea.

mistakes.why: Reading the two passages together is exactly what causes mix-ups about who said what. Read and label each passage alone first, then compare.
Careful reading helps, but the rule is about order: finish and label one passage alone before you start the other, so you keep the writers straight.

screens.title: Purpose: genre clues
screens.html:
Paired passages often have different purposes, and the GED asks about that difference. There are four common purposes:

PurposeCommon genresLanguage clues
Informnews report, fact sheet, textbookthird person, numbers, several views
Explainhow-to, science or history articlebecause, as a result, steps
Persuadeeditorial, letter to the editor, speechshould, must, strong words, a request
Narrate or reflectmemoir, diary, personal story“I,” scenes, feelings

The genre is your first clue. The language is your second.

check.prompt:
Choose the purpose each kind of text usually has.

A county fact sheet about a new recycling schedule is usually written to {{0}}.

A letter to the editor about the same schedule is usually written to {{1}}.

A memoir about growing up near the town dump is usually written to {{2}}.
check.hint: Think about who usually writes each genre and what that writer wants from the reader.
check.explain: A fact sheet informs: neutral facts, dates, and rules. A letter to the editor persuades: it argues for a view. A memoir narrates and reflects: it tells the writer's own story and what it meant.

options: inform
persuade
narrate and reflect
why: A fact sheet from the county gives dates and rules in a neutral voice. It does not argue for a position, so its purpose is to inform.
A fact sheet tells no personal story. It reports facts about the schedule, so its purpose is to inform.

options: inform
persuade
narrate and reflect
why: A letter to the editor is an opinion genre. Writers send them to argue for a view, so the usual purpose is to persuade.
A letter may include a personal story, but its job is to convince readers or officials of something. The usual purpose is to persuade.

options: inform
persuade
narrate and reflect
why: A memoir is told in first person about the writer's own life. It is not a neutral report of facts.
A memoir may lead readers to feel something, but its main job is to tell a personal story and reflect on it, not to argue for a position.

screens.title: Inform or persuade? Read the ending
screens.html: A text can inform and still lean toward a side, so look for stronger signals of persuasion: the writer states a position (“X is a mistake”), uses strong language (“a wall across the best water”), or asks the reader to do something. The ending is the best tiebreaker. A writer who wants something from you usually asks for it in the last lines.

example.prompt:
Text A (county fact sheet): The Mill Creek Dam was built in 1911 to power a sawmill that closed in 1958. Removing it next summer will cost an estimated $2.1 million; repairing its cracked spillway would cost $3.4 million. Removal will reopen about 12 miles of creek to migrating fish.

Text B (fishing guide's blog): I've guided trips on Mill Creek for twenty years, and that dam is a wall across the best water in the county. Taking it out is the best news this creek has had in a century. Come see the difference next fall.

How do the purposes differ?
steps: Label A: county · the removal plan, its costs and results · neutral voice, numbers, no request. Purpose: inform.
Label B: fishing guide · removal is great news · “I,” strong words, and an invitation at the end. Purpose: express support and persuade.
Notice that both texts end up favoring removal, but for different reasons and with different jobs.
example.answer: Text A informs readers about the plan and its costs; Text B shares an enthusiastic personal view to win support for removal.

check.prompt:
Text A (water department notice): Starting July 1, lawn watering is limited to two days a week. The reservoir is at 58 percent of capacity.

Text B (gardener's letter): Two days a week will kill every young tree planted this spring. The city should allow hand-watering of new trees on any day. Write to the council before July 1.

Which statement best describes the purposes of the two texts?
check.hint: Check the last line of each text. Does either writer ask the reader to do something?
check.explain: Text A is a notice: a rule, a date, and a fact, with no opinion. Its purpose is to inform. Text B states a position (“will kill every young tree”), says what the city “should” do, and ends with a request (“Write to the council”). Its purpose is to persuade readers to push for an exception. The tempting wrong answer says both texts persuade, but the notice takes no position.
options: Text A informs residents about a new rule; Text B tries to get readers to push for an exception.
Text A persuades residents to plant fewer trees; Text B informs readers about the reservoir level.
Both texts try to persuade readers to oppose the new limits on lawn watering this summer.
Text A tells a personal story about the drought; Text B explains how reservoir levels are measured.
why: This swaps the details. The notice never mentions planting trees, and the reservoir level appears in Text A, not Text B.
Text A states a rule and a fact in a neutral voice; it does not oppose anything. Only Text B argues, and it asks for an exception, not an end to the limits.
Text A is a notice with no “I” and no story, and Text B never explains how levels are measured. Check the genre and the language before choosing.

screens.title: Point of view: who, what, what's at stake
screens.html:
To compare points of view, ask three questions about each writer:

  1. Who is speaking? A reporter, an expert, a worker, a family member? First person (“I”) or third person? An insider who lives the issue, or an outsider who studies it?
  2. What does the speaker believe about the topic?
  3. What is at stake for the speaker? What could they gain or lose?

A stake shapes what a writer notices and what they leave out. It does not make the writer wrong. Judging a writer only by their stake is last week's attack-on-the-person error. Note the stake, then judge the evidence.

Also watch for writers who agree with part of the other side. That is called a concession, and it often appears right before the word but.

check.prompt:
“I've worked night shifts at Bayview Hospital for nine years. The new $8 daily parking fee costs me $160 a month. The hospital says the garage needs repairs, and I believe it. But charging the people who keep the hospital running isn't the answer.”

Select two statements that accurately describe the writer's point of view.
check.hint: Find the sentence where she agrees with the hospital. What comes right after it?
check.explain: The writer works at the hospital and pays the fee herself, so she is an insider with a stake. She concedes that the garage needs repairs (“and I believe it”), then turns with But to her real point: staff should not be charged. A reader who skips the concession may wrongly think she denies the repairs are needed.
options: The writer is an insider with a personal stake in the parking fee.
The writer accepts that the garage needs repairs but opposes charging staff for them.
The writer is a reporter who presents both sides without taking one.
The writer believes the garage does not really need any repairs.
The writer wants the hospital to close the garage for good.
why: The writer uses “I,” describes her own shifts and costs, and states a position (“isn't the answer”). A neutral reporter would not do any of those things.
This is the opposite of what she says: “The hospital says the garage needs repairs, and I believe it.” That sentence is a concession.
Nothing in the paragraph mentions closing the garage. She objects to who pays for repairs, not to the garage itself.

screens.title: Reporting a view is not holding it
screens.html:
News reports often quote people who disagree. A reporter who quotes a farmer opposing a new highway is reporting the farmer's view, not holding it. To find a news writer's own point of view, ask:

  • Does the writer present more than one side?
  • Are opinions inside quotation marks and credited to someone (“said Ruth Ambrose”)?
  • Does the writer ever say, in their own words, what should happen?

If the opinions all belong to people being quoted, the report is informing, even when one quote is especially moving. Save “the article supports…” for articles where the writer takes a position in their own voice.

check.skill: Point of view in a news report
check.prompt:
“The council will vote Tuesday on a plan to close the Fifth Street pool. ‘This pool is where my kids learned to swim,’ said resident Lena Park, who opposes the plan. Parks director Sam Ruiz said repair costs of $900,000 make closing the pool ‘the responsible choice.’”

Which statement best describes the point of view of this news report?
check.hint: Whose words are inside the quotation marks? Does the writer ever give an opinion in their own words?
check.explain: Every opinion in the report is inside quotation marks and credited to a person: Park opposes the plan, and Ruiz supports it. The writer never states a view in their own words. So the report presents both sides without taking one. The most tempting wrong answer picks the more emotional quote and treats it as the writer's opinion.
options: It reports views from both sides without stating a view of its own.
It opposes closing the pool, as Lena Park's quote about her children shows.
It supports closing the pool, as the parks director's quote about cost shows.
It is told by Lena Park, a resident whose children learned to swim at the pool.
why: Park's words are inside quotation marks and credited to her. Quoting someone who opposes the plan is reporting her view, not holding it.
Ruiz's words are also a quote credited to him. The report gives both sides and never says in its own voice what the council should do.
The report is in third person and names Park as someone it quotes (“said resident Lena Park”). She is a source, not the writer.

screens.title: When one text is a story
screens.html:
The GED sometimes pairs an informational text with a literary one: a history with a memoir, or an article with a diary. The questions are the same, but the answers often follow a pattern:

History or articleMemoir or diary
Point of viewthird person, outsidefirst person, inside
Scopegeneral: many people, many yearsspecific: one person, one place
Purposeinform or explainnarrate and reflect

Usually the personal text adds what the experience felt like, and sometimes it complicates the general account with a moment that does not fit.

example.prompt:
Text A (textbook): The Erie Canal opened in 1825. It linked the Hudson River to Lake Erie and cut the cost of shipping goods between New York City and the Great Lakes region.

Text B (a canal worker's diary, written for this lesson): Walked the towpath twelve hours today behind the mules. My boots are through at the heel. Captain says we reach Buffalo by Thursday if the locks are clear.

How do the texts differ, and what does B add?
steps: Text A: third person, general, about a whole region. Purpose: inform.
Text B: first person, one worker, one day. Purpose: record personal experience.
B does not disagree with A. It adds what the work was like, which A never covers.
example.answer: A explains why the canal mattered; B adds one worker's experience of the hard daily labor behind it.

check.prompt:
Passage 1 (history): In the 1930s and 1940s, many rural families got electricity for the first time through member-owned electric cooperatives. The lines reached farms that private power companies had skipped because the farms were too far apart.

Passage 2 (memoir, written for this lesson): The night the lights came on, my mother stood at the switch for a full minute before she flipped it. Then she sat down at the kitchen table and cried.

What does Passage 2 add to Passage 1?
check.hint: Which kind of information can only a first-person memory provide?
check.explain: Passage 1 gives the general history: who got power and why it took cooperatives. Passage 2 is a first-person memory of one moment in one family. It adds the human experience: the mother's pause at the switch and her tears. The tempting wrong answer, the reason companies skipped farms, is real information, but it comes from Passage 1.
options: It shows what getting electricity for the first time felt like for one family.
It explains why private power companies did not build lines out to many farms.
It gives the number of farm families who got electricity through cooperatives.
It argues that the cooperatives charged rural families too much for electric power.
why: That explanation (the farms were too far apart) is in Passage 1. The question asks what Passage 2 adds.
Neither passage gives a number of families. Passage 2 is about one mother on one night.
Passage 2 never mentions prices or cooperatives. Nothing in the memoir is an argument.

screens.title: Kinds of evidence
screens.html:
To compare two writers' evidence, first name what kind each one uses:

  • Statistics and data: numbers, surveys, records. “Crashes fell from 41 to 27, according to the city's traffic report.”
  • Expert statements: quotes from people who work or study in the field. “A pediatrician at Mercy Hospital says…”
  • Anecdotes: short personal stories. “My neighbor kept a library book for six months.”
  • Examples: specific cases that illustrate a point.
  • Unsupported generalizations: broad claims with no proof. “Everyone knows drivers ignore those signs.”

Often one passage leans on data and quotes while the other leans on personal experience. Naming the types is the first step to judging which is stronger.

check.prompt: Drag each piece of evidence to the kind of evidence it is.
check.hint: Ask: is it a number, a qualified person, one person's story, or a big claim with no proof?
check.explain: The health department figure is a statistic from a named source. The pediatrician is an expert speaking about her field. The brother's story is an anecdote: one case. “Everyone knows… never work” is an unsupported generalization: it claims something about everyone with no proof.
choices: “The state health department reports that 14 percent of adults smoke.”
“‘Teens need about nine hours of sleep,’ says a pediatrician at Mercy Hospital.”
“My brother quit smoking after one week of the program.”
“Everyone knows programs like this never work.”
check.why: The most common mix-up is the brother's story: because it describes a real result, students call it data. It is one person's experience, an anecdote. Statistics describe many cases with numbers.

screens.title: Whose evidence is stronger?
screens.html:
Strong evidence is specific, relevant to the exact claim, and from a source you could check. Weak evidence includes words like everyone, always, nobody, one anecdote used to prove something about a whole group, and predictions with no support.

The most powerful move on paired passages: sometimes one passage's evidence directly tests the other passage's claim.

example.prompt:
Text A (library director): Two years ago, the Pine Hollow Library stopped charging late fees. Since then, 1,140 cardholders whose accounts had been blocked for fines have returned to borrowing, and the share of books returned within a month of the due date has stayed at about 96 percent.

Text B (resident's letter): Getting rid of late fees was a mistake. Everyone knows people only return things on time when there's a penalty. My neighbor kept a library book for half a year.

Which text has stronger evidence?
steps: List A: two specific numbers from library records over two years.
List B: “everyone knows” (no proof) and one neighbor's story.
Test: if fines were needed, the return rate should have dropped. They stayed at about 96 percent, so A's data contradicts B's claim.
example.answer: Text A. Its specific, relevant data directly answers B's worry; B relies on a generalization and one anecdote.

check.prompt:
Passage 1 (transit agency): Daily ridership on Route 7 rose from 2,100 to 3,400 in the six months after buses began running every 10 minutes, according to fare-card records.

Passage 2 (letter): Nobody wanted more frequent buses. I ride Route 7 every day, and it's as empty as ever.

Which statement best compares the evidence in the two passages?
check.hint: Which passage could you check? Which uses a word like “nobody”?
check.explain: Passage 1 gives specific numbers (2,100 to 3,400 riders a day), a source (fare-card records), and a time span (six months). Passage 2 uses “nobody,” an unsupported generalization, and one rider's impression. The tempting wrong answer trusts the daily rider, but one person on a few trips cannot see what thousands of fare cards show.
options: Passage 1 is stronger: it gives specific numbers from records over six months.
Passage 2 is stronger because its writer rides Route 7 and sees the buses daily.
They are equally strong because each comes from a source that knows Route 7.
Passage 1 is weaker because a transit agency can never report its own numbers honestly.
why: Riding one bus a day lets the writer see a few trips, not the whole route over six months. Firsthand experience feels convincing, but it cannot outweigh fare-card records.
Knowing the route is not the same as having equal evidence. One gives measured counts; the other gives an impression and the word “nobody.”
An agency may want its program to look good, and that is worth noticing. But “can never” is an overgeneralization, and records-based numbers can be checked.

screens.title: Synthesize: agree, disagree, add, complicate
screens.html:
To synthesize is to put two sources together into a fuller understanding. Two texts can relate in four ways. Remember them as ADAC:

  • Agree: both texts support the same point.
  • Disagree: the texts make opposite claims.
  • Add: one text gives new information that fits with the other.
  • Complicate: one text shows that the other's point is not the whole story by adding a limit, an exception, or a cost.

Real pairs often do more than one: they agree on a fact and complicate the conclusion. When a question asks how two texts relate, name the relationship in your own words before you read the choices.

check.prompt:
Passage 1 claims: “The city's new tree-planting program will cool hot neighborhoods.”

Drag each statement from a different Passage 2 to show how it relates to Passage 1.
check.hint: For each statement, ask: same point, opposite point, new fact that fits, or a problem that makes the point less simple?
check.explain: The shade statement supports the same point: Agree. The pavement statement says the opposite: Disagree. The 4,000 trees statement is new, compatible information: Add. The watering statement accepts the idea but shows a cost or limit: Complicate.
choices: “Shade from street trees can lower sidewalk temperatures by many degrees, so the program should help cool hot blocks.”
“Planting trees will not cool these neighborhoods at all; the heat comes from pavement, not from a lack of shade.”
“The program will plant 4,000 trees, mostly oaks and maples, over the next five years.”
“Trees can cool streets, but young trees need watering for three years, and the program has no money for that.”
check.why: Students most often swap Add and Complicate. The number and kinds of trees fit Passage 1 without changing its point (Add). The watering problem accepts that trees cool streets but shows a limit that could keep the program from working (Complicate).

screens.title: Add or complicate?
screens.html:
Add and complicate are the two relationships readers mix up most. Both bring in new information. The difference is what that information does to the first text's point:

Add

New facts that fit. The first text's point stays just as simple and just as true.

P1: “The library opens a new branch Monday.” P2: “The branch has a children's room and a study area.”

Complicate

A limit, exception, or cost. The first text's point is still partly true, but it is no longer the whole story.

P1: “The new branch will serve the whole east side.” P2: “No bus line reaches it.”

Test: after reading Passage 2, would you still state Passage 1's point the same way? If not, Passage 2 complicates it.

check.prompt:
Passage 1: “The new Elm Street branch library opens Monday with 20 public computers, making it easier for job seekers to apply for work online.”

Passage 2: “Great news about the computers. But the branch closes at 5 p.m., before most people with day jobs can get there.”

Does Passage 2 add to Passage 1 or complicate it? Type one word.
check.hint: After reading Passage 2, would you still state Passage 1's point exactly the same way?
check.explain: Passage 2 accepts the good news (“Great news about the computers”) but adds a limit: the branch closes before many workers can get there. After reading it, you would no longer say simply that the branch makes things easier for job seekers. That is complicate. It is not add, because the new fact pushes against Passage 1's point.

mistakes.why: Passage 2 does bring new information, but it is a limit: the 5 p.m. closing keeps many working job seekers from using the computers. That makes Passage 1's point less simple, so it complicates.
Passage 2 does not make an opposite claim; it calls the computers “great news.” It accepts the point and shows a limit, so it complicates.

screens.title: “Both passages” questions: the two-check rule
screens.html:
The GED often asks, “Which statement is supported by both passages?” The most common wrong answer is a choice that is true but appears in only one passage. It feels right because you remember reading it.

The two-check rule: before choosing, put your finger on a line in Passage 1 and a line in Passage 2 that support the choice. If you can find it in only one, cross it out.

example.prompt:
Text A (shelter flyer): Adopting an adult dog from Riverbend Animal Shelter costs $75 and includes vaccines and a microchip. Adult dogs are often already house-trained.

Text B (veterinarian's column): Shelter dogs can make wonderful pets, and adult dogs are often calmer than puppies. Still, plan for food, checkups, and supplies; they usually add several hundred dollars in the first year.

Which do both texts support: “Adult shelter dogs can be good pets” or “Adult dogs are calmer than puppies”?
steps: “Good pets”: A says adult dogs are often house-trained; B says shelter dogs can make wonderful pets. Found in both.
“Calmer than puppies”: found in B. Search A: it never compares adults with puppies. B only.
example.answer: “Adult shelter dogs can be good pets.” The calmness choice is true, but only for Text B.

check.prompt:
Passage 1 (school district notice): Beginning this month, every district high school serves free breakfast in the cafeteria from 7:15 to 7:45 a.m.

Passage 2 (student column): Free breakfast is a great idea, and I've already seen more of my friends eating before first period. But 7:45 is too early to stop serving; the east side buses don't arrive until 7:50.

Which statement is supported by both passages?
check.hint: For each choice, find a line in Passage 1. Then find a line in Passage 2. Both lines must exist.
check.explain: Run the two-check rule. Passage 1: every high school “serves free breakfast.” Passage 2: “Free breakfast is a great idea… more of my friends eating.” Both support free breakfast is being served. The bus time is true but appears only in Passage 2, so it fails the rule even though it feels familiar.
options: The district's high schools are serving free breakfast to students.
Buses from the east side of the district arrive at school at 7:50 a.m.
Breakfast should be served every morning until at least 8:00 a.m.
More students are eating breakfast this year than did last year.
why: This is true, but only Passage 2 mentions the buses. It fails the two-check rule.
Passage 1 sets the time at 7:45 and argues nothing. Passage 2 says 7:45 is too early but never names 8:00. This is not stated by either.
Only Passage 2 says more friends are eating, and neither passage compares this year with last year.

screens.title: “One passage only” questions
screens.html:
Some questions ask for information that appears in one passage but not the other, or ask you to sort statements into “Passage 1 only,” “Passage 2 only,” and “Both.” Do the two-check rule in reverse:

  1. Find the detail in the passage the question names.
  2. Search the other passage for the same detail, even in different words.
  3. If you find it there too, it belongs in “Both,” not “only.”

These questions often reveal something important: what a writer chose to leave out. A writer arguing one side may skip the facts that would most help the other side.

check.prompt:
Passage 1 (news report): Greenfield will add a traffic signal at the Pine and Third crosswalk after two pedestrians were hit there this year. The signal will cost $85,000 and will be installed in April.

Passage 2 (crossing guard's letter): I've guarded the Pine and Third crossing for six years. The signal is welcome, but April is too late; it gives the school only two months of use before summer. Until then, the city should lower the speed limit near the school.

Select two statements that appear in Passage 2 but not in Passage 1.
check.hint: For each choice, look for it in Passage 1. If you find it there, cross it out.
check.explain: Search Passage 1 for each choice. The signal and the April date appear in both passages. The $85,000 cost is in Passage 1 only. The guard's six years on the job and the call to lower the speed limit appear only in Passage 2.
options: The writer has worked at the crossing for six years.
The city should lower the speed limit near the school.
A traffic signal will be added at Pine and Third.
The signal will be installed in April.
The signal will cost $85,000.
why: Both passages say this: Passage 1 reports the plan, and Passage 2 calls the signal “welcome.”
Both passages mention April: Passage 1 gives the date, and Passage 2 says April is too late.
Only Passage 1 gives the cost. The question asks for details found in Passage 2 but not Passage 1.

screens.title: “How does Passage 2 relate to Passage 1?”
screens.html:
For these questions, use ADAC before you read the choices:

  1. What is Passage 1's main point?
  2. What does Passage 2 do to that point: agree, disagree, add, or complicate? Often it is a mix, such as “agrees on the facts but complicates the conclusion.”
  3. Say it in one sentence. Then find the choice that matches.

Wrong choices usually overstate the relationship (“contradicts” when Passage 2 only points out a limit) or claim there is no connection at all.

example.prompt:
Text A (company report): During a six-month trial, Harlan Logistics moved its office staff to a four-day week with no cut in pay. Sick days fell 22 percent, and the number of employees who quit dropped from 14 to 5.

Text B (warehouse supervisor): The four-day week has been great for the office. But my team runs the loading dock, and trucks arrive six days a week. The company needs a plan for workers whose jobs don't fit a four-day schedule.

How does Text B relate to Text A?
steps: A's point: the four-day week worked for office staff.
B agrees (“great for the office”) but points out workers the program does not fit.
That is agree and complicate: a limit the report does not mention.
example.answer: Text B agrees that the program worked for the office and complicates the report by showing it does not fit every job.

check.prompt:
Passage 1 (company report): After the warehouse switched to four 10-hour shifts a week, overtime costs fell 18 percent.

Passage 2 (worker's letter): The new schedule saved the company money, and I like the long weekend. But the last two hours of a 10-hour shift on the loading dock are brutal, and two of us have hurt our backs since March.

How does Passage 2 relate to Passage 1?
check.hint: Find the sentence where the worker agrees with the report. Then look at what comes after “But.”
check.explain: Passage 1's point: the new schedule cut overtime costs. Passage 2 agrees (“saved the company money”) and then shows a cost the report leaves out: exhausting final hours and two back injuries. That is agree and complicate. The “contradicts” choice overstates the relationship; the worker never disputes the savings.
options: It agrees the schedule saved money but complicates the report by showing a cost to workers.
It contradicts the report by showing that overtime costs went up under the new schedule.
It repeats the report's figures about overtime and adds nothing that the report leaves out.
It has no real connection to the report, since it is about injuries rather than schedules.
why: Passage 2 says the opposite: “The new schedule saved the company money.” It accepts the report's finding.
Passage 2 gives no figures, and it adds something new: injuries on long shifts.
The injuries happened on the new 10-hour shifts, so they are directly connected to the schedule the report describes.

screens.title: Concessions: where writers agree with the other side
screens.html:
A concession is a point where a writer admits the other side is right about something. Writers concede to seem fair, and then they turn back to their own argument. Signal words include I admit, I'll grant, it's true that, of course, granted, maybe it does, usually followed by but, still, however.

Concessions matter on paired passages because they show where two opposing writers actually agree. That is often the answer to a “both passages” question. They also keep you from the trap of assuming opposing writers disagree about everything.

check.prompt: Click the sentence in which the writer concedes a point to the other side.
check.hint: Look for a signal phrase like “I admit,” followed by a turn word in the next sentence.
check.explain: “I admit that the building is old and that repairs would be expensive” grants the strongest reason for closing the school; that is a concession. The signal is “I admit,” and the next sentence turns back with “But.” The first sentence is the writer's claim, and the last is a recommendation.
spans: The plan to close Lincoln Elementary is a mistake.
I admit that the building is old and that repairs would be expensive.
But closing it would mean forty-minute bus rides for children who now walk.
Families chose this neighborhood because of this school.
The board should look for repair grants before it votes.
check.why: Students sometimes click the first sentence because it states a position. That is the writer's claim, not a concession. A concession admits something that helps the other side, such as the cost of repairs.

screens.title: Writing about two texts
screens.html:
When you write about paired passages, in a short answer or in the extended response, use transitions that show how the texts relate:

To show…Use
likenesssimilarly, likewise, both, also
differencein contrast, however, on the other hand, while, whereas
a concessionalthough, even though, granted

Also watch agreement when you write about two writers. Both takes a plural verb (“Both writers agree”), but each, either, and neither take a singular verb (“Each writer agrees”).

check.prompt:
Choose the option that correctly completes each sentence.

Passage 1 presents the downtown parking plan as a success. {{0}} Passage 2 argues that the plan has hurt small stores.

Each of the writers {{1}} that traffic downtown has increased.
check.hint: For the first blank, are the two views alike or different? For the second, find the true subject of the sentence.
check.explain: Blank 1: the two passages take opposite views, so the transition must show difference: “In contrast,” Blank 2: the subject is “Each,” not “writers,” so the verb is singular: “Each of the writers agrees.” The most tempting wrong answer is “agree,” which matches the nearby plural word “writers.”

options: In contrast,
Similarly,
For example,
Therefore,
why: “Similarly” signals a likeness, but “a success” and “has hurt small stores” are opposite views.
“For example” introduces an example of the previous point. Passage 2's view is not an example of Passage 1's; it is a different view.
“Therefore” signals a result. Passage 2's argument is not caused by Passage 1's view; it differs from it.

options: agrees
agree
are agreeing
have agreed
why: The subject is “Each,” which is singular; “of the writers” only describes it. A singular subject needs “agrees.”
“Are agreeing” is plural. The subject “Each” is singular.
“Have agreed” is plural. With the singular subject “Each,” it would be “has agreed.”

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
Here are the rules to carry into Practice:

  • Read each passage alone first and label it: who is writing, the main point, and the purpose.
  • Compare on four points: claim, purpose (inform, explain, persuade, narrate and reflect), point of view (who, what they believe, what is at stake), and evidence.
  • Reporting a view is not holding it. A stake shapes a writer's view but does not make it wrong.
  • Stronger evidence is specific, relevant, and sourced. Weaker evidence uses “everyone” or “always,” one anecdote, or no source. One passage's evidence can test the other's claim.
  • Synthesize with ADAC: Agree, Disagree, Add, Complicate. Many pairs agree on facts and complicate conclusions.
  • “Both” questions need the two-check rule. “Only” questions need the reverse search.
  • Look for concessions: they show where opposing writers agree.

Next: Practice Set A (15 questions). Score 80% or higher on first tries to master it; otherwise take Set B. Then take the Exit Check.

stimuli.title: Paired Passages: Slower Streets
stimuli.html:
Passage 1: Ashford Weighs a 20 mph Limit on Neighborhood Streets

(1) The Ashford City Council will vote next month on whether to lower the speed limit on most residential streets from 30 miles per hour to 20. The change would not affect major roads such as Route 9 or Harbor Avenue, which would keep their current limits. If the measure passes, the city would replace about 2,400 speed limit signs over six months at an estimated cost of $380,000.

(2) The proposal grew out of a one-year pilot program. Beginning last spring, the city posted 20 mph signs in six neighborhoods and tracked what happened. According to a report by the city's traffic engineering office, reported crashes on the pilot streets fell from 41 in the year before the pilot to 27 during the pilot year. Crashes that injured a pedestrian or cyclist fell from 9 to 4. Average driving speeds, measured by roadside sensors, dropped from 27 miles per hour to 24.

(3) Supporters say those numbers point in a clear direction. Traffic safety researchers have long found that the speed of a vehicle strongly affects how badly a person on foot is hurt in a collision; a pedestrian struck at 20 miles per hour is far more likely to survive than one struck at 30. “Three miles per hour doesn't sound like much,” said Dana Okafor, a parent who helped organize residents in one pilot neighborhood. “But on a street full of kids, it's the difference between a close call and a tragedy.”

(4) Not everyone is convinced. The Ashford Business Association has asked the council to delay the vote. In a letter to council members, the association argued that slower limits could lengthen delivery and service routes and that drivers may simply ignore signs that do not match the feel of the road. The association recommended physical changes, such as speed humps and raised crosswalks, on the streets with the most crashes.

(5) City traffic engineer Paul Reyes urged caution in reading the pilot results. “One year is a short window, and six neighborhoods is a small sample,” Reyes said. “Crash numbers bounce around from year to year, so we can't say for sure how much of the drop came from the new limit.” Reyes added that his office would recommend combining lower limits with physical changes on the most dangerous streets, if the council approves funding for both.

(6) Residents can comment on the proposal at a public hearing at City Hall on the evening of March 14 or by writing to the city clerk before that date.

Passage 2: A Driver's View: Fix the Dangerous Streets, Not Every Street

by Marcus Bell

(1) I have driven a delivery van in Ashford for fourteen years. I know which corners hide children chasing a ball, which alleys back onto school bus stops, and which streets turn into racetracks after five o'clock. So when I say that a citywide 20 mph limit is the wrong answer, I am not saying that speeding is fine. I am saying that we should spend our money where the danger actually is.

(2) Supporters of the plan point to the city's pilot program, and I'll admit that crashes on the pilot streets went down, which I'm glad to see. But look closer at the report. Average speeds dropped by only three miles per hour. Drivers did not slow down to 20; they slowed down a little, and then they went back to driving the way the road told them to drive. A wide, straight street with no parked cars feels like a 30 mph street, and a sign will not change that feeling.
