(3) Every driver I know thinks the new signs are a waste. On my route, I watch cars pass the 20 mph signs in the pilot zone every single day without touching the brakes. If a rule is going to be broken by nearly everyone, it is not really a rule. It is a decoration.

(4) Meanwhile, the city plans to spend $380,000 on new signs. That money could pay for about sixty speed humps on the streets where kids actually get hurt. Speed humps don't need drivers to agree with them. You either slow down or you rattle your teeth loose. The same goes for raised crosswalks near schools and narrower lanes on the streets that invite speeding.

(5) Slower limits also have a cost that the planners don't count. A few extra minutes on each delivery adds up across a whole day. For drivers like me who are paid by the route, not by the hour, that time comes out of our own pockets. Small businesses that run service vans will pay, too, and they will pass those costs on to customers.

(6) I want my neighbors' children to get home safely as much as anyone on the council does. That is exactly why I am asking the council to vote no on the citywide limit and yes on fixing the streets we already know are dangerous. Put the money into concrete, not into signs.

stimuli.title: Paired Passages: The Last Lighthouse Keepers
stimuli.html:
Passage 1: When the Lights Went Automatic

(1) For most of the nineteenth century, every working lighthouse on the American coast depended on a person. Keepers climbed the tower at dusk to light the lamp, and they stayed awake through the night to keep it burning. They trimmed wicks so the flame would not smoke, polished the great glass lens so its beam would carry for miles, and in many towers wound the clockwork that turned the lens. Each morning, they recorded the weather, the condition of the light, and any passing ships in a logbook.

(2) The work was steady and often lonely. Many stations sat on rocky islands or remote points of land, and keepers frequently lived there with their families. When a keeper died or became ill, a wife or daughter sometimes took over the job, and a number of women were appointed as keepers in their own right.

(3) In the early twentieth century, technology began to change the job. Electric lamps replaced oil, and electric motors replaced hand-wound clockwork. Later, devices that switched a light on at dusk and off at dawn removed the need for anyone to tend the lamp at all. In 1939, responsibility for the nation's lighthouses passed to the U.S. Coast Guard, which gradually converted the stations to automatic operation. By the end of the 1990s, nearly every lighthouse in the country ran without a resident keeper.

(4) The main reasons for the change were cost and reliability. Paying and housing a keeper at a remote station was expensive, and supplying an island station by boat could be difficult in bad weather. Automatic equipment, by contrast, could run for long periods with only occasional visits from maintenance crews. Automated lights are typically equipped with backup batteries and spare lamps that switch on by themselves if the main lamp fails.

(5) Today, many former keepers' houses stand empty or have been turned into museums. The lights themselves still shine, now watched over by sensors and checked by crews who arrive by truck or boat a few times a year. By most measures, automation did what it was meant to do: it kept the lights burning at a fraction of the cost.

Passage 2: The Winter the Light Stopped Needing Us

(1) I was eleven the winter the Coast Guard came to automate the light at Gannet Point. My father had kept that light for nineteen years, and his father had kept it before him. I had never lived anywhere else. Our kitchen window looked straight up at the tower, and I fell asleep most nights counting the slow sweep of the beam across my ceiling: one, two, three, dark.

(2) The technicians arrived in early December with crates of gray equipment. They were polite young men who called my father “sir” and me “miss,” and they asked him where the fuses were kept. My father showed them everything. He showed them the logbooks, too, forty-one of them on a shelf by the stairs, every one filled in his small, square handwriting or his father's. One of the technicians flipped through a book from 1952 and whistled. “You wrote down every ship?” he asked. “Every one I saw,” my father said.

(3) I remember one night that February, after the new equipment was running but before we had moved out. A storm took down the power line from the mainland, and the backup battery that was supposed to take over did not. The tower went black. My father was up the stairs with a lantern and the old kerosene lamp before I had my boots on. He kept the light going by hand until dawn, and in the morning he wrote it all down in the logbook, the way he always had. Nobody from the Coast Guard ever asked to see that entry.

(4) We left Gannet Point in April. On our last evening, my father stood at the kitchen window and watched the beam come on by itself at dusk. He did not say anything for a long time. Then he said, mostly to himself, “Well. It doesn't need me anymore.” He sounded proud and something else, something I didn't have a word for at eleven.

(5) People tell me automation was the sensible choice, and I believe them. The numbers were on its side. But I also know that for one night in February, the light at Gannet Point stayed lit because a man was awake to climb the stairs.
stimuli.source: Both passages were written for this course. Passage 2 is a work of fiction.

stimuli.title: Draft Response: Two Views on Slower Streets
stimuli.html:
A GED student wrote this draft response comparing the two Slower Streets passages. It contains blanks where the student is deciding between word choices.

(1) Both passages discuss Ashford's plan to lower the speed limit on residential streets to 20 miles per hour. The news article in Passage 1 explains the proposal and reports what people on each side think. (A) the opinion piece in Passage 2 argues against the plan from the point of view of a delivery driver.

(2) The two passages use some of the same evidence. Each of the writers (B) the city's pilot program and the $380,000 cost of new signs. However, they use that evidence differently. Passage 1 reports the numbers and lets the city engineer warn that one year is a short time. Bell uses the same numbers to argue that the signs did not work.

(3) Bell also raises a cost that Passage 1 does not fully explain. He points out that drivers who are paid by the route lose money when (C) trips take longer. Passage 1 mentions the business association's worry about longer routes, (D) it never says who would pay that cost.

(4) In my view, Passage 1 gives the more reliable picture. Bell's experience as a driver is real, but (E) not enough to prove that nearly every driver ignores the signs. His claim that $380,000 could pay for sixty speed humps also has no source.

stimuli.title: Paired Passages: A Later Start for High School
stimuli.html:
Passage 1: Dalton County Weighs Later Start for High Schools

(1) The Dalton County School Board will vote in April on whether to move the start of the school day at its five high schools from 7:15 a.m. to 8:30 a.m. beginning next fall. Elementary schools would start earlier, at 7:45 a.m., so that the district could keep using the same buses for both. The district estimates that the change would cost about $640,000 a year, mostly for extra bus drivers on routes that cannot be shared.

(2) The plan follows a one-year pilot at two high schools, Westbrook and Pine Ridge. According to a district report, first-period tardies at the two schools fell from 2,860 in the year before the pilot to 1,730 during the pilot year. Students who took a sleep survey in both years reported getting an average of 34 more minutes of sleep on school nights. The share of first-period grades that were D or F dropped from 19 percent to 14 percent.

(3) Doctors who study adolescent sleep have long reported that teenagers' body clocks shift during puberty, making it hard for many to fall asleep before 11 p.m. “Asking a sixteen-year-old to be alert at 7:15 is like asking an adult to take a test at 5 a.m.,” said Dr. Alicia Moreno, a pediatrician who spoke in support of the plan at a board meeting.

(4) Some parents and coaches have raised concerns. The Dalton County Athletic Boosters said in a statement that a later dismissal would push practices and games into the evening and cause athletes to miss more class time when they travel to away games. Some parents who work early shifts worry about leaving younger children at the bus stop before sunrise.

(5) District research director Kevin Liu said the pilot results are encouraging but limited. “Two schools for one year is a small sample, and the students who answered the survey both years may not represent everyone,” Liu said. “We would want to keep measuring if the board approves the change districtwide.”

(6) The board will hold a public hearing on March 20. Families can also submit comments through the district website.

Passage 2: A Coach's View: Look at the Whole Day

by Denise Harlow

(1) I have coached girls' basketball at Pine Ridge High School for eleven years, and I was there for every day of the later-start pilot. I want my players rested and healthy. So when I say the board should not move every high school to an 8:30 start, I am not saying sleep doesn't matter. I am saying the plan creates problems the district has not solved.

(2) I'll grant that tardies went down during the pilot, and my first-period colleagues noticed the difference. But look at what happened at the other end of the day. School let out at 3:45 instead of 2:30. Our practices ran until 6:15, and on game days my players got home after 9:00 with homework still to do. Some of them were getting less sleep on those nights, not more.

(3) Every athlete I know was more tired this year than last. Two of my starters told me they were falling asleep in their last class on game days. And when we traveled to away games, players had to leave school at 1:00, missing their last two classes instead of one.

(4) The district says the change will cost $640,000 a year. That money could hire a full-time tutor at every high school to help students who struggle in early classes. Tutors would help every student, not just the night owls.

(5) There are also families to consider. If elementary schools start at 7:45, little kids will be standing at bus stops in the dark all winter. Many parents in my neighborhood leave for work at 6:30 and will have no one to wait with their children.

(6) I respect the doctors who study sleep. But a plan that looks good on a chart has to work in real lives too. I am asking the board to vote no on a districtwide change and instead to try a later start one or two days a week, so we can see whether the benefits hold up without upending every family's schedule.
stimuli.source: Both passages were written for this course.

stimuli.title: Paired Passages: When the Switchboards Went Quiet
stimuli.html:
Passage 1: From Switchboards to Dial Tones

(1) In the early days of the telephone, no call went through without a person in the middle. A caller lifted the receiver and waited for a switchboard operator to answer. The caller gave the name or number of the person they wanted, and the operator connected the two lines by plugging a cord into the right jack on a large board. In small towns, a single operator often ran the switchboard from a back room of a store or of her own home.

(2) Operators did more than connect calls. Because they knew the people on their lines, they often passed along messages, told callers where a doctor could be found, and sounded the alarm when there was a fire.

(3) Automatic switching equipment changed the job. Inventors had built machines that could connect calls without an operator as early as the 1890s, and through the twentieth century telephone companies replaced manual switchboards with dial systems, starting with large cities. Callers now turned a dial to send the number themselves, and the machinery made the connection. Small rural exchanges were often among the last to change; some kept their hand-operated boards into the 1970s.

(4) The main reasons for the change were cost and speed. A dial system could handle a great many calls at once, day and night, without paying a staff of operators. Calls went through in seconds. For emergencies and special requests, callers could still dial “0” to reach an operator, who now worked in a central office that served many towns.

(5) Few people today remember the sound of an operator asking, “Number, please?” By most measures, the dial system did exactly what it promised: it made calling faster and cheaper for millions of people.

Passage 2: The Night the Board Went Dark

(1) My mother ran the switchboard in Alder Creek for twenty-two years, from a back room of our house with a window onto Main Street. I was her only daughter, and I grew up falling asleep to the soft click of her cords and the sound of her voice saying, “Number, please?” She knew every family on the board by their ring and most of them by their cough.

(2) The telephone company came to convert Alder Creek to dial the spring I turned twelve. Two men in coveralls spent a week installing gray cabinets in a new brick building by the feed store. They were friendly, and one of them asked my mother to show him how the old board worked. She showed him everything, including the notebook where she kept track of who was sick, who was traveling, and which farms had no one home during the day.

(3) Three weeks after the new system started, the Pruitts' barn caught fire at two in the morning. Mrs. Pruitt dialed “0,” as the company had told everyone to do. The operator who answered was in an office sixty miles away. She asked for a street address, and the Pruitts had never had one; everybody just called it the place past the second bridge. Mrs. Pruitt hung up and called our house instead. My mother was awake before the second ring. She called the fire chief, then three neighbors with water trucks, all by memory.

(4) When the old board was finally carted away, my mother stood in the empty back room for a long time. “Well,” she said, “nobody needs me to say ‘number, please’ anymore.” She didn't sound sad, exactly. She sounded like someone counting what had been gained and what had been lost.

(5) People tell me the dial system was progress, and I agree. Calls are faster, and nobody has to sit up all night beside a board. But I also know that one night in Alder Creek, help found the Pruitts because a woman was awake who knew the way.
stimuli.source: Both passages were written for this course. Passage 2 is a work of fiction.

stimuli.title: Draft Response: Two Views on a Later School Start
stimuli.html:
A GED student wrote this draft response comparing the two passages about a later start for high school. It contains blanks where the student is deciding between word choices.

(1) Both passages discuss Dalton County's plan to start high school at 8:30 a.m. The news article in Passage 1 describes the plan and reports the views of supporters and critics. (A) the opinion piece in Passage 2 argues against the plan from the point of view of a basketball coach.

(2) The two writers rely on some of the same facts. Neither of them (B) that first-period tardies went down during the pilot. However, they draw different conclusions from the pilot. Passage 1 lets the district's research director explain that the sample was small, while Harlow focuses on what happened after school.

(3) Harlow also points to a problem that the article mentions only briefly. She explains that practices ran late and that some athletes lost sleep on (C) nights. Passage 1 reports the boosters' concern about evening games, (D) it does not describe how late athletes actually got home.

(4) In my view, Passage 1 gives the more reliable picture. Harlow's experience is real, but (E) not enough to prove that every athlete was more tired.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of Passage 1?
items.hint: Look at the type of text it is and at whose views it reports. Does the writer ever say what the council should do?
items.explain:
Step 1. Identify the genre. Passage 1 is a news article: it gives facts (the vote, the cost, the pilot data) and quotes several people.

Step 2. Check whose views appear. Paragraph 3 presents supporters, paragraph 4 presents the business association's objections, and paragraph 5 presents the engineer's caution. The writer never says what the council should do.

Step 3. A text that reports facts and several sides without taking one is written to inform. The choice about informing readers of the proposed change and the views for and against it is correct.

The “persuade the council” choice confuses quoting a supporter (Dana Okafor) with being a supporter. The “criticize” choice is wrong because the article reports the association's view without judging it. The sensors choice is too narrow; sensors are mentioned once, in paragraph 2.
options: to inform readers about a proposed speed limit change and the views for and against it
to persuade the city council to approve the 20 mph limit before the March public hearing
to criticize the Ashford Business Association for asking the council to delay its vote
to explain how the city's roadside sensors measure the speeds of cars on residential streets
why: This confuses quoting a supporter with being one. The article quotes Dana Okafor, but it also gives the business association's objections and the engineer's caution, and it never says what the council should do.
The article reports the association's request and its reasons without judging them. Reporting a view is not criticizing it.
This is too narrow. Sensors are mentioned once, in paragraph 2, as the source of the speed data; they are not what the article is about.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses Marcus Bell's main claim in Passage 2?
items.hint: Read the last two sentences of paragraph 1 and the request in paragraph 6.
items.explain:
Step 1. Find where Bell states his position. Paragraph 1 ends: “we should spend our money where the danger actually is.” Paragraph 6 asks the council to “vote no on the citywide limit and yes on fixing the streets we already know are dangerous.”

Step 2. Combine those statements: spend on fixing dangerous streets, not on a citywide limit. That matches the choice about spending on physical changes to the most dangerous streets instead of a citywide limit. Correct.

The choice that speeding is not a serious problem is the opposite of what Bell says: “I am not saying that speeding is fine.” The pilot choice contradicts paragraph 2, where Bell admits crashes went down. The pay choice twists a detail from paragraph 5; Bell mentions being paid by the route to show a cost of slower limits, not to argue for a change in pay.
options: Speeding on residential streets is not a serious problem anywhere in Ashford.
Ashford should fix its most dangerous streets instead of lowering the limit citywide.
The city's pilot program had no effect at all on the number of crashes on pilot streets.
Delivery drivers in Ashford should be paid by the hour instead of by the route they drive.
why: This is the opposite of Bell's view. He says, “I am not saying that speeding is fine,” and he wants money spent “where the danger actually is.”
Bell admits the opposite in paragraph 2: “I'll admit that crashes on the pilot streets went down.” His point is that speeds dropped only a little.
This twists a detail from paragraph 5. Bell mentions being paid by the route to show a cost of slower limits, not to argue for a change in how drivers are paid.

items.prompt: The sentences below are from paragraph 2 of Passage 2. Click the sentence in which Bell concedes (admits) a point that helps the other side of the argument.
items.hint: Look for a signal phrase such as “I'll admit” and ask whether the fact it introduces helps supporters of the lower limit.
items.explain:
Step 1. A concession is a point the author admits is true even though it helps the other side.

Step 2. The first sentence uses the signal phrase “I'll admit” and states that crashes on the pilot streets went down. Fewer crashes is the strongest evidence for the lower limit, so admitting it helps the other side. Correct.

Step 3. Check the others. “But look closer at the report” is the turn back to Bell's own argument. The sentence about speeds dropping “only three miles per hour” is a fact Bell uses to support his side; the word “only” shows he is downplaying it. The last two sentences are Bell's own reasoning.
spans: Supporters of the plan point to the city's pilot program, and I'll admit that crashes on the pilot streets went down, which I'm glad to see.
But look closer at the report.
Average speeds dropped by only three miles per hour.
Drivers did not slow down to 20; they slowed down a little, and then they went back to driving the way the road told them to drive.
A wide, straight street with no parked cars feels like a 30 mph street, and a sign will not change that feeling.
items.why: Many students click “Average speeds dropped by only three miles per hour” because it is a fact about the pilot. But Bell uses it to support his own side; the word “only” downplays the change. The concession is the sentence with “I'll admit.”

items.prompt: Which statement is supported by information in both passages?
items.hint: Use the two-check rule: find a line in Passage 1 and a line in Passage 2 for the same choice.
items.explain:
Step 1. Test each choice in Passage 1, then in Passage 2.

Step 2. Crashes went down: Passage 1, paragraph 2 reports crashes fell from 41 to 27. Passage 2, paragraph 2: “I'll admit that crashes on the pilot streets went down.” Both passages support it. Correct.

Step 3. The other choices fail the two-check rule. “Main cause” is not supported by either passage; in fact, the engineer in Passage 1 says “we can't say for sure how much of the drop came from the new limit.” The claim that drivers “did not slow down at all” goes beyond both passages: Bell himself says drivers “slowed down a little,” and Passage 1's sensor data shows average speeds did drop. Higher prices for customers is Bell's prediction in Passage 2 only.
options: The 20 mph limit was the main cause of the drop in crashes on the pilot streets.
Most drivers in the pilot zone did not slow down at all when they passed the signs.
The number of crashes on the pilot streets went down during the pilot year.
Slower speed limits will raise the prices that Ashford customers pay for services.
why: Neither passage says this. In Passage 1 the engineer warns, “we can't say for sure how much of the drop came from the new limit,” and Bell doubts the signs did much.

Neither passage supports “not at all.” Bell says drivers “slowed down a little,” even though he describes cars passing the signs without braking, and Passage 1's sensor data shows average speeds dropped from 27 to 24 miles per hour.
This is Bell's prediction in paragraph 5 of Passage 2. Passage 1 never mentions prices, so it fails the two-check rule.

items.prompt: Select two pieces of information that appear in Passage 1 but are not mentioned in Passage 2.
items.hint: For each choice, look for it in Passage 2. If you find it there, cross it out.
items.explain:
Step 1. Confirm every choice appears in Passage 1. All five do: injury crashes (paragraph 2), the engineer's warning (paragraph 5), speeds from 27 to 24 (paragraph 2), $380,000 (paragraph 1), and speed humps (paragraph 4, from the business association).

Step 2. Now search Passage 2 for each.

  • Injury crashes falling from 9 to 4: Passage 2 never gives this number. Correct.
  • The engineer's warning: Bell never mentions the engineer or the length of the pilot. Correct.
  • Speeds dropping three miles per hour: Bell says “Average speeds dropped by only three miles per hour” (paragraph 2). Appears in both.
  • $380,000: Bell names this cost in paragraph 4. Appears in both.
  • Speed humps: Bell's main solution in paragraph 4. Appears in both.

Notice that Bell leaves out the two details that would most help the other side: the drop in injury crashes and the engineer's balanced explanation.
options: Crashes that injured a pedestrian or cyclist fell from 9 to 4.
The city engineer warned that one year of data is too short to be sure what caused the drop in crashes.
Average driving speeds dropped by about three miles per hour.
Replacing the signs would cost about $380,000.
Speed humps could be used to slow traffic on dangerous streets.
why: Bell writes, “Average speeds dropped by only three miles per hour” (Passage 2, paragraph 2). This detail appears in both passages.
Bell names the $380,000 cost of new signs in paragraph 4 of Passage 2. It appears in both passages.
Speed humps are Bell's main solution in paragraph 4 of Passage 2. They appear in both passages.

items.prompt: Drag each statement into the correct category to show which passage it describes.
items.hint: Passage 1 is a news report; Passage 2 is a personal opinion piece. Check each statement against both before placing it.
items.explain:
Passage 1 only: “Quotes a city official.” Passage 1 quotes traffic engineer Paul Reyes (paragraph 5). Passage 2 quotes no one.

Passage 2 only: “Uses the writer's own experience” (Bell's fourteen years of driving and what he sees on his route). “Ends with a direct request to the city council” (“I am asking the council to vote no…”); Passage 1 ends with information about the public hearing, not a request. “Drivers who are paid by the route will lose money” (paragraph 5 of Passage 2). Passage 1 mentions that the business association worries about longer routes, but it never mentions drivers being paid by the route.

Both passages: The cost of the signs ($380,000 appears in paragraph 1 of Passage 1 and paragraph 4 of Passage 2) and the drop in crashes (paragraph 2 of each).
choices: Uses the writer's own experience as evidence
Quotes a city official
Mentions the cost of replacing the signs
Ends with a direct request to the city council
Reports that crashes went down on the pilot streets
Argues that drivers who are paid by the route will lose money
items.why: The most common error is putting “Ends with a direct request to the city council” in Both. Passage 1 ends with information about the public hearing, which is not a request; only Bell asks the council to vote a certain way.

items.skill: Transitions of comparison; agreement; confused words
items.prompt:
Read the student's draft response. Then choose the option that correctly completes each blank in these excerpts.

Paragraph 1, blank (A): {{0}} the opinion piece in Passage 2 argues against the plan from the point of view of a delivery driver.

Paragraph 2, blank (B): Each of the writers {{1}} the city's pilot program and the $380,000 cost of new signs.

Paragraph 4, blank (E): Bell's experience as a driver is real, but {{2}} not enough to prove that nearly every driver ignores the signs.
items.hint: For (A), ask whether the sentence shows a likeness or a difference from the sentence before it. For (B), find the true subject. For (E), try reading the blank as “it is.”
items.explain:
Blank (A). Step 1: The sentence before says Passage 1 “explains the proposal and reports what people on each side think.” Step 2: This sentence says Passage 2 “argues against the plan.” Explaining both sides and arguing one side are different, so the transition must show contrast: “In contrast,” Correct. “Similarly” signals a likeness, “For example” signals an example of the previous point, and “As a result” signals an effect; none fits.

Blank (B). Step 1: The subject is “Each,” not “writers”; “of the writers” is a phrase that describes it. Step 2: “Each” is singular, and the paragraph is in present tense (“use,” “reports”). Step 3: A singular, present-tense verb is needed: “Each of the writers mentions.” Correct. “Mention,” “are mentioning,” and “have mentioned” are all plural forms.

Blank (E). Step 1: The sentence needs a subject and a verb: “but it is not enough.” Step 2: The contraction of “it is” is “it's.” Correct. “Its” shows ownership (“the dog wagged its tail”) and would leave the clause without a verb. “Its'” is not a word in standard English.

options: In contrast,
Similarly,
For example,
As a result,
why: “Similarly” signals that the next idea is like the one before. Explaining both sides and arguing one side are different, so a likeness transition does not fit.
“For example” introduces an example of the previous point. Passage 2 is not an example of Passage 1; it is a different kind of text with a different purpose.
“As a result” signals an effect. Passage 1's explaining the plan did not cause Bell to argue against it.

options: mention
mentions
are mentioning
have mentioned
why: “Mention” is plural. The subject is “Each,” which is singular; “of the writers” only describes it.
“Are mentioning” is plural, and the subject “Each” is singular.
“Have mentioned” is plural. A singular subject would need “has mentioned,” and the paragraph is in the present tense (“use,” “reports”).

options: it's
its
its'
why: “Its” shows ownership (“the dog wagged its tail”). The sentence needs a subject and a verb, “it is,” so it needs the contraction “it's.”
“Its'” is not a word in standard English. The contraction of “it is” is “it's.”

items.prompt:
Read paragraph 3 of the student's draft response. Then choose the option that correctly completes each blank.

Blank (C): He points out that drivers who are paid by the route lose money when {{0}} trips take longer.

Blank (D): Passage 1 mentions the business association's worry about longer routes, {{1}} it never says who would pay that cost.
items.hint: For (C), who do the trips belong to? For (D), are the two ideas a cause and effect, or a contrast?
items.explain:
Blank (C). The word must show that the trips belong to the drivers. “Drivers” is plural, so the plural possessive is “their.” “There” is a place word, “they're” means “they are,” and “its” is singular.

Blank (D). The sentence sets two ideas against each other: Passage 1 does mention the worry about longer routes, but it does not say who pays. A contrast word is needed: “but.” “So” and “because” show cause and effect, which does not fit, and “for example” would create a comma splice.

options: their
there
they're
its
why: “There” points to a place (“over there”) or starts a sentence (“There is”). The sentence needs a word that shows the trips belong to the drivers.
“They're” means “they are.” “When they are trips take longer” makes no sense; the sentence needs the possessive “their.”
“Its” is singular, but it refers back to “drivers,” which is plural. The plural possessive is “their.”

options: but
so
because
for example
why: “So” signals a result, but leaving out who pays is not a result of mentioning the worry. The two ideas contrast: it mentions one thing but skips another.
“Because” signals a reason. The article does not skip the cost because it mentions the worry; the ideas are in contrast.
“For example” cannot join two complete sentences with only a comma (that makes a comma splice), and the second idea is not an example of the first.

items.prompt: How does the purpose of Passage 2 differ from the purpose of Passage 1?
items.hint: Label each passage: who is writing, and is the passage about the whole country or one place?
items.explain:
Step 1. Label Passage 1. It is written in third person, covers lighthouses “on the American coast” over more than a century, and gives causes (“The main reasons for the change were cost and reliability”). Its purpose is to inform and explain.

Step 2. Label Passage 2. It is told in first person (“I was eleven”) by a keeper's daughter about one station, Gannet Point, and reflects on what the change meant to her family. Its purpose is to narrate and reflect.

Step 3. The choice that says Passage 1 explains how and why lighthouses were automated while Passage 2 shares one family's experience matches both labels. Correct.

The choice about Passage 1 arguing that automation was a mistake gets both passages wrong: Passage 1 calls automation a success, and Passage 2 does not simply defend it. The choice that gives Passage 1 the family story and Passage 2 the general history swaps the passages. The museum choice is not stated; museums are mentioned once in Passage 1, and neither passage urges readers to do anything.
options: Passage 1 argues that automation was a mistake, while Passage 2 defends the decision to automate the lights.
Passage 1 tells the story of one keeper's family, while Passage 2 gives a general history of American lighthouses.
Passage 1 explains how and why lighthouses were automated, while Passage 2 shares one family's experience of it.
Passage 1 urges readers to visit lighthouse museums, while Passage 2 urges readers to join the Coast Guard.
why: This gets both passages wrong. Passage 1 says automation “did what it was meant to do,” and the narrator of Passage 2 accepts it as sensible but also feels a loss; she does not simply defend it.
This swaps the passages. The single family's story is Passage 2 (“I was eleven”); the general history is Passage 1.
Neither passage urges readers to do anything. Museums are mentioned once in Passage 1, and the Coast Guard technicians in Passage 2 are simply part of the story.

items.prompt: Which statement best compares the two passages' points of view on automation?
items.hint: Compare the last paragraph of each passage. What does each writer say automation accomplished, and how does the narrator of Passage 2 feel?
items.explain:
Step 1. Passage 1's view: its last sentence says, “By most measures, automation did what it was meant to do: it kept the lights burning at a fraction of the cost.” That presents automation as a success.

Step 2. Passage 2's view: the narrator says, “People tell me automation was the sensible choice, and I believe them.” But she also describes her father sounding “proud and something else” and ends with the night a person had to keep the light lit. She accepts the decision but feels a loss.

Step 3. The choice that says Passage 1 presents automation as a success while the narrator accepts it as sensible but feels a loss captures both views. Correct.

The choice that both passages present automation as a loss is wrong because Passage 1 does not present automation as a loss, and the narrator of Passage 2 says she believes it was sensible. The Coast Guard choice is not supported: Passage 1 simply reports what the Coast Guard did, and Passage 2 describes the technicians as polite but does not praise the Coast Guard. The emotion choice reverses the passages: Passage 2 is the emotional one.
options: Both passages present automation as a loss that should not have happened at all.
Passage 1 presents it as a success; the narrator accepts it was sensible yet feels a loss.
Passage 1 is critical of the Coast Guard, while the narrator of Passage 2 praises its technicians.
Passage 1 shows strong personal emotion, while Passage 2 avoids expressing any feelings.
why: Passage 1 calls automation a success (“did what it was meant to do”), and the narrator of Passage 2 says she believes it was “the sensible choice.” Neither treats it as a mistake.
Passage 1 simply reports what the Coast Guard did, without criticism. Passage 2 describes the technicians as polite but never praises the Coast Guard.
This reverses the passages. Passage 1 is a neutral history; Passage 2 is full of feeling, such as the father sounding “proud and something else.”

items.prompt: Which statement best compares how the two Slower Streets passages use evidence?
items.hint: List the kinds of evidence in each passage. Then look for any claim in Passage 2 that has no source.
items.explain:
Step 1. List Passage 1's evidence: crash and speed numbers from the city's traffic engineering report (paragraph 2), a research finding about pedestrian survival (paragraph 3), and quotations from a parent, the business association, and the city engineer (paragraphs 3–5).

Step 2. List Passage 2's evidence: Bell's fourteen years of driving and what he sees on his route (paragraphs 1 and 3), one number taken from the city report (the three-mile-per-hour drop), and claims with no source: “Every driver I know thinks the new signs are a waste” (an unsupported generalization) and “That money could pay for about sixty speed humps” (no source given).

Step 3. The choice that says Passage 1 relies on a city report and several sources while Passage 2 relies on the writer's observations and some unsourced claims matches both lists. Correct.

The choice that Passage 1 uses only statistics and Passage 2 only expert quotations is wrong twice: Passage 1 also uses quotations, and Passage 2 quotes no experts. The choice that both passages rely mainly on personal stories is wrong because Passage 1 is built on data. The choice that Passage 2 is more reliable because its writer drives every day is the trap of judging evidence by the writer's experience; daily observation by one driver cannot show what drivers across the pilot zone did, which is what the sensor data measures.
options: Passage 1 relies only on statistics from the city's report, while Passage 2 relies only on quotations from traffic safety experts.
Both passages rely mainly on personal stories from Ashford residents and drivers rather than on data from the city's pilot program.
Passage 2 uses more reliable evidence than Passage 1 because its writer has driven Ashford's streets every day for fourteen years.
Passage 1 rests mainly on city data and quotes from several people; Passage 2 rests on Bell's observations and unsourced claims.
why: This is wrong twice: Passage 1 also quotes a parent, the business association, and the engineer, and Passage 2 quotes no experts at all.
Passage 1 is built on data from the city's traffic engineering report (crashes, injury crashes, sensor speeds). Only Passage 2 leans on personal experience.
This judges evidence by the writer's experience. One driver's daily view cannot show what drivers across the whole pilot zone did; the roadside sensors measured that.

items.skill: Synthesis: how one text relates to another
items.prompt: How does the information in paragraph 5 of Passage 1 relate to Bell's argument in Passage 2?
items.hint: Reread paragraph 5 sentence by sentence. Which parts would Bell agree with? Is there any part he would not?
items.explain:
Step 1. Summarize paragraph 5. The engineer says one year and six neighborhoods are too little data to know “how much of the drop came from the new limit.” He would recommend “combining lower limits with physical changes on the most dangerous streets.”

Step 2. Compare with Bell. Bell doubts that the signs work and wants physical changes on dangerous streets. The engineer's doubt and his support for physical changes agree with Bell. But the engineer wants lower limits too, while Bell asks the council to vote no on the limit. So the paragraph partly supports Bell and partly complicates his argument.

Step 3. The choice that says paragraph 5 partly supports Bell describes this mixed relationship. Correct.

The “fully supports” choice is wrong because the engineer never recommends rejecting the limit. The “contradicts” choice is wrong because the engineer says the opposite: “we can't say for sure.” The “no connection” choice is wrong because paragraph 5 does not discuss sign costs at all.
options: It fully supports Bell, because the engineer recommends that the council reject the lower limit and pay for speed humps instead.
It partly supports Bell: the engineer doubts the limit alone explains the drop and favors physical changes, but alongside lower limits.
It contradicts Bell, because the engineer says the lower limit was clearly the main cause of the drop in crashes on the pilot streets.
It has no connection to Bell's argument, because the engineer discusses only the cost of replacing the city's speed limit signs.
why: The engineer never recommends rejecting the limit. He says his office would recommend “combining lower limits with physical changes,” which keeps the lower limit.
The engineer says the opposite: “we can't say for sure how much of the drop came from the new limit.”
Paragraph 5 does not mention sign costs at all. It is about how to read the pilot results and what the engineer's office would recommend.

items.skill: Synthesis: how one text complicates another
items.prompt: How does the event described in paragraph 3 of Passage 2 complicate a claim made in Passage 1?
items.hint: First, summarize what happens in paragraph 3 of Passage 2. Then find the sentence in Passage 1 that the event challenges.
items.explain:
Step 1. Summarize paragraph 3 of Passage 2: a storm cut the power, “the backup battery that was supposed to take over did not,” and the father kept the light going by hand until dawn.

Step 2. Find the related claim in Passage 1. Paragraph 4 says automated lights have “backup batteries and spare lamps that switch on by themselves if the main lamp fails.”

Step 3. The memoir shows a case where that backup did not work and a human was needed. It does not prove Passage 1 wrong in general, but it shows the claim is not the whole story. That is what complicate means. The choice about the failed backup battery and the person who kept the light going is correct.

The other choices misstate Passage 2. The father did not sleep; he “was up the stairs with a lantern.” The Coast Guard did come; its technicians installed the equipment in December. The father did not stop his logbook; “in the morning he wrote it all down in the logbook, the way he always had.”
options: Passage 1 says keepers stayed awake through the night, but Passage 2 shows that the narrator's father slept through the storm.
Passage 1 says the Coast Guard took over lighthouses in 1939, but Passage 2 shows that the Coast Guard never came to Gannet Point.
Passage 1 says automated lights have backups that switch on by themselves, but in Passage 2 the backup failed and a person kept the light lit.
Passage 1 says keepers recorded events in logbooks, but Passage 2 shows the narrator's father stopped keeping his logbook after automation.
why: The father did not sleep. Paragraph 3 says he “was up the stairs with a lantern and the old kerosene lamp before I had my boots on.”
The Coast Guard did come: “I was eleven the winter the Coast Guard came to automate the light,” and its technicians installed the equipment in December.
The father kept writing: “in the morning he wrote it all down in the logbook, the way he always had.”

items.prompt:
Complete each statement about the two lighthouse passages.

Paragraph 4 of Passage 1 says automated lights have backup batteries that switch on by themselves. The storm in paragraph 3 of Passage 2 {{0}} that claim.

Both passages show that {{1}}.

Passage 2 {{2}} Passage 1 by showing what the change meant to one keeper's family.
items.hint: For each blank, use ADAC. For the middle blank, use the two-check rule: find a line in each passage.
items.explain:
Blank 1. Passage 1 says automated lights have backups that “switch on by themselves.” In Passage 2, “the backup battery that was supposed to take over did not,” and a person had to keep the light lit. That does not prove Passage 1 wrong in general, but it shows the claim is not the whole story: it complicates it.

Blank 2. Passage 1: by the end of the 1990s, “nearly every lighthouse in the country ran without a resident keeper.” Passage 2: the Coast Guard automates Gannet Point, the family moves out, and the father says, “It doesn't need me anymore.” Both show lighthouses came to run without resident keepers. Museums appear only in Passage 1.

Blank 3. The memoir gives the inside, personal view of a change that Passage 1 describes from the outside. It adds to Passage 1 without disagreeing with it.

options: complicates
proves
repeats
has nothing to do with
why: The storm shows a backup that did not work, so it cannot prove that backups switch on by themselves. It shows the claim is not the whole story.
Passage 2 does not restate the claim; it describes a night when the backup failed, which pushes against the claim.
The storm is about a backup battery that failed, which is exactly what Passage 1's claim is about.

options: lighthouses came to run without resident keepers
automated lights never fail
automation was a mistake that should be undone
keepers' houses were turned into museums
why: Passage 2 shows a failure, and Passage 1 mentions backup equipment for when a lamp fails. Neither says automated lights never fail.
Neither passage says this. Passage 1 calls automation a success, and the narrator of Passage 2 believes it was “the sensible choice.”
Only Passage 1 mentions museums (paragraph 5). Passage 2 never says what happened to the keeper's house, so this fails the two-check rule.

options: adds to
disagrees with
summarizes
corrects
why: The narrator accepts that automation was sensible, so Passage 2 does not take the opposite side. Its family story is new information that fits the history.
A summary would restate Passage 1's main points. Passage 2 tells a new, personal story that Passage 1 never includes.
Passage 2 does not say Passage 1 got its facts wrong. A family's experience of the change adds a personal side to the history.

items.prompt: Select two ideas that both the author of Passage 1 and the narrator of Passage 2 would accept.
items.hint: An idea counts only if you can point to support for it in Passage 1 and in Passage 2.
items.explain:
Use the two-check rule on each idea.

  • Automation made sense because of cost: Passage 1 says the main reasons were “cost and reliability” and that automation kept the lights burning “at a fraction of the cost.” The narrator says, “People tell me automation was the sensible choice, and I believe them. The numbers were on its side.” Both accept it.
  • Keepers kept written records: Passage 1 says keepers recorded the weather, the light, and passing ships “in a logbook.” Passage 2 describes forty-one logbooks and the father writing down every ship. Both.

The idea that automated equipment needs no human help is the most tempting wrong choice, but the storm in Passage 2 is a direct example of a human being needed, and Passage 1 mentions visiting maintenance crews.
options: Automating the lights made sense because it cost less.
Keepers kept written records of what happened at their stations.
Automated equipment can run forever without any human help.
Keeping a lighthouse was mostly exciting and social work.
The Coast Guard should return keepers to the lighthouses.
why: Passage 2 shows the opposite: when the backup failed, a person had to keep the light lit. Even Passage 1 mentions maintenance crews who visit a few times a year.
Passage 1 calls the work “steady and often lonely,” and nothing in Passage 2 makes it sound exciting or social; the father's work is long nights of tending the light.
Neither writer calls for this. The narrator says she believes automation was sensible; she only notes what was lost.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of Passage 1?
items.hint: What kind of text is Passage 1? Does the writer ever say, in their own words, what the board should do?
items.explain:
Step 1. Identify the genre. Passage 1 is a news article: it gives facts (the vote, the cost, the pilot results) and quotes several people.

Step 2. Check whose views appear. Paragraph 3 presents a supporter, Dr. Moreno. Paragraph 4 presents the boosters' and parents' concerns. Paragraph 5 presents the research director's caution. The writer never says what the board should do.

Step 3. A text that reports facts and several sides without taking one is written to inform.

The most tempting wrong answer says the article persuades the board, because Dr. Moreno's quote is vivid. But quoting a supporter is not the same as being one.
options: to inform readers about a proposed later start time and the views for and against it
to persuade the school board to approve the 8:30 start before the March 20 public hearing
to criticize the Athletic Boosters for raising concerns about late practices and away games
to explain why teenagers' body clocks make it hard for many of them to fall asleep early at night
why: This confuses quoting a supporter with being one. The article quotes Dr. Moreno, but it also reports the boosters' and parents' concerns and the research director's caution, and it never says how the board should vote.
The article reports the boosters' statement without judging it. Reporting a view is not criticizing it.
This is too narrow. Teen body clocks come up in paragraph 3 as background for the plan; the article is about the proposed change and the debate over it.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses Denise Harlow's main claim in Passage 2?
items.hint: Read the end of paragraph 1 and the request in paragraph 6.
items.explain:
Step 1. Find where Harlow states her position. Paragraph 1: “the board should not move every high school to an 8:30 start.” Paragraph 6: “I am asking the board to vote no on a districtwide change and instead to try a later start one or two days a week.”

Step 2. Combine them: reject the districtwide change and test a smaller version. That is her main claim.

The tempting wrong answer says sleep does not matter, because Harlow argues against a plan meant to help students sleep. But she says directly that she is “not saying sleep doesn't matter.” Her objection is to this plan's side effects.
options: The board should reject a districtwide 8:30 start and test a later start one or two days a week.
Sleep does not really matter very much for teenagers who play school sports at Pine Ridge.
The later-start pilot had no effect at all on first-period tardies at Pine Ridge High School.
Elementary schools in Dalton County should start later in the morning than the five high schools do.
why: This is the opposite of Harlow's view. She writes, “I am not saying sleep doesn't matter,” and “I want my players rested and healthy.”
Harlow admits the opposite in paragraph 2: “I'll grant that tardies went down during the pilot.”
This twists paragraph 5. Harlow worries about young children at bus stops in the dark, but she never proposes changing elementary start times; her request is about the high school plan.

items.prompt: The sentences below are from paragraph 2 of Passage 2. Click the sentence in which Harlow concedes (admits) a point that helps the other side of the argument.
items.hint: Look for a signal phrase such as “I'll grant” and ask whether the fact it introduces helps supporters of the later start.
items.explain:
Step 1. A concession is a point the writer admits is true even though it helps the other side.

Step 2. “I'll grant that tardies went down during the pilot” uses a signal phrase (“I'll grant”) and admits a result that supports the later start. That is the concession.

Step 3. “But look at what happened…” is the turn back to Harlow's own argument. The sentences about dismissal time, late practices, and lost sleep are her evidence against the plan.
spans: I'll grant that tardies went down during the pilot, and my first-period colleagues noticed the difference.
But look at what happened at the other end of the day.
School let out at 3:45 instead of 2:30.
Our practices ran until 6:15, and on game days my players got home after 9:00 with homework still to do.
Some of them were getting less sleep on those nights, not more.
items.why: Some students click “Some of them were getting less sleep on those nights, not more” because it sounds like an admission. It is actually Harlow's own evidence against the plan. The concession is the sentence with “I'll grant.”

items.prompt: Which statement is supported by information in both passages?
items.hint: Use the two-check rule: find a line in Passage 1 and a line in Passage 2 for the same choice.
items.explain:
Step 1. Test each choice in Passage 1, then in Passage 2.

Step 2. Tardies went down: Passage 1, paragraph 2 reports first-period tardies fell from 2,860 to 1,730. Passage 2, paragraph 2: “I'll grant that tardies went down during the pilot.” Both passages support it.

Step 3. The other choices fail the two-check rule. No passage says the later start was the main cause of better grades. Less sleep for athletes and the tutor idea appear only in Passage 2. The less-sleep choice is especially tempting because Harlow says it strongly, but Passage 1's survey points the other way for students overall.
options: The later start was the main reason that first-period grades improved.
Athletes got less sleep during the pilot year than in the year before.
First-period tardies went down at the pilot schools during the pilot.
Hiring tutors would help more students than a later start would help.
why: Neither passage says the later start caused the improvement. Passage 1's research director warns that two schools for one year is a small sample, and Passage 2 never mentions grades.
This is Harlow's claim in Passage 2, and only about some athletes on game nights. Passage 1's survey found that students reported 34 more minutes of sleep. It fails the two-check rule.
This is Harlow's idea in paragraph 4 of Passage 2. Passage 1 never mentions tutors, so it fails the two-check rule.

items.prompt: Select two pieces of information that appear in Passage 1 but are not mentioned in Passage 2.
items.hint: For each choice, look for it in Passage 2, even in different words. If you find it there, cross it out.
items.explain:
Step 1. Confirm that every choice appears in Passage 1. All five do: the sleep survey and tardies (paragraph 2), the director's warning (paragraph 5), the cost and the 7:45 elementary start (paragraph 1).

Step 2. Search Passage 2 for each.

  • 34 more minutes of sleep: Harlow never mentions the survey. Correct.
  • The director's warning: Harlow never mentions Kevin Liu or the sample size. Correct.
  • Tardies went down: conceded in paragraph 2. Both.
  • $640,000: paragraph 4. Both.
  • 7:45 elementary start: paragraph 5. Both.

Notice that Harlow leaves out the survey result that most helps the other side, much as a writer arguing one side often does.
options: Students reported getting an average of 34 more minutes of sleep on school nights.
The research director warned that two schools for one year is a small sample.
First-period tardies went down at the pilot schools during the pilot year.
The change would cost the district about $640,000 a year.
Elementary schools would start earlier, at 7:45 a.m.
why: Harlow writes, “I'll grant that tardies went down during the pilot” (Passage 2, paragraph 2). This appears in both passages.
Harlow repeats the $640,000 figure in paragraph 4 of Passage 2. It appears in both passages.
Harlow writes, “If elementary schools start at 7:45…” in paragraph 5 of Passage 2. It appears in both passages.

items.prompt: Drag each statement into the correct category to show which passage it describes.
items.hint: Passage 1 is a news report; Passage 2 is an opinion piece. Check each statement against both passages before placing it.
items.explain:
Passage 1 only: “Quotes a doctor who supports the plan.” Passage 1 quotes Dr. Alicia Moreno (paragraph 3). Passage 2 only says Harlow respects sleep doctors.

Passage 2 only: “Uses the writer's own experience” (eleven years of coaching, what happened to her players). “Ends with a direct request to the school board” (“I am asking the board to vote no…”); Passage 1 ends with information about the hearing. “Proposes spending the money on tutors” (paragraph 4).

Both passages: the yearly cost ($640,000 in paragraph 1 of Passage 1 and paragraph 4 of Passage 2) and the drop in tardies (paragraph 2 of each).
choices: Quotes a doctor who supports the plan
Uses the writer's own experience as evidence
Mentions the yearly cost of the change
Ends with a direct request to the school board
Reports that first-period tardies went down
Proposes spending the money on tutors instead
items.why: The most common error is putting “Quotes a doctor who supports the plan” in Both. Harlow mentions “the doctors who study sleep,” but she quotes no one; only Passage 1 quotes Dr. Moreno.

items.skill: Transitions of comparison; agreement; confused words
items.prompt:
Read the student's draft response. Then choose the option that correctly completes each blank in these excerpts.

Paragraph 1, blank (A): {{0}} the opinion piece in Passage 2 argues against the plan from the point of view of a basketball coach.

Paragraph 2, blank (B): Neither of them {{1}} that first-period tardies went down during the pilot.

Paragraph 4, blank (E): Harlow's experience is real, but {{2}} not enough to prove that every athlete was more tired.
items.hint: For (A), does the sentence show a likeness or a difference from the sentence before it? For (B), find the true subject. For (E), try reading the blank as “it is.”
items.explain:
Blank (A). The sentence before says Passage 1 “describes the plan and reports the views of supporters and critics.” This sentence says Passage 2 “argues against the plan.” Those are different approaches, so the transition must show contrast: “In contrast,”

Blank (B). The subject is “Neither,” not “them.” Neither is singular, and the paragraph is in the present tense, so the verb is “denies.” “Deny” is the most tempting wrong answer because it matches the nearby plural word “them.”

Blank (E). The clause needs a subject and verb: “but it is not enough.” The contraction is “it's.” “Its” shows ownership, and “its'” is not a word.

options: In contrast,
Similarly,
For example,
As a result,
why: “Similarly” signals a likeness. Reporting both sides and arguing against the plan are different approaches, so a likeness transition does not fit.
“For example” introduces an example of the previous point. Passage 2 is not an example of Passage 1; it is a different kind of text.
“As a result” signals an effect. The news article did not cause Harlow to argue against the plan.

options: denies
deny
are denying
have denied
why: “Deny” is plural. The subject is “Neither,” which is singular; “of them” only describes it.
“Are denying” is plural, and the subject “Neither” is singular.
“Have denied” is plural. A singular subject would need “has denied,” and the paragraph is in the present tense.

options: it's
its
its'
why: “Its” shows ownership (“the team lost its coach”). The sentence needs a subject and a verb, “it is,” so it needs the contraction “it's.”
“Its'” is not a word in standard English. The contraction of “it is” is “it's.”

items.prompt:
Read paragraph 3 of the student's draft response. Then choose the option that correctly completes each blank.

Blank (C): She explains that practices ran late and that some athletes lost sleep on {{0}} nights.

Blank (D): Passage 1 reports the boosters' concern about evening games, {{1}} it does not describe how late athletes actually got home.
items.hint: For (C), is “nights” singular or plural? For (D), are the two ideas a cause and effect, or a contrast?
items.explain:
Blank (C). The word points to the plural noun “nights,” so it must be plural and able to describe a noun: “those nights.” “Them” cannot describe a noun, and “that” and “this” are singular.

Blank (D). The sentence sets two ideas against each other: Passage 1 does report the concern, but it does not give the details. A contrast word is needed: “but.” “So” and “because” show cause and effect, and “for example” would create a comma splice.

options: those
them
that
this
why: “Them” is an object pronoun and cannot describe a noun; “them nights” is nonstandard English.
“That” is singular, but “nights” is plural. The plural form is “those.”
“This” is singular, but “nights” is plural. A plural noun needs “those” (or “these”).

options: but
so
because
for example
why: “So” signals a result, but leaving out how late athletes got home is not a result of reporting the concern. The ideas contrast.
“Because” signals a reason. The article does not skip the details because it reports the concern; the ideas are in contrast.
“For example” cannot join two complete sentences with only a comma (that makes a comma splice), and the second idea is not an example of the first.

items.prompt: How does the purpose of Passage 2 differ from the purpose of Passage 1?
items.hint: Label each passage: who is telling it, and is it about the whole country or one town?
items.explain:
Step 1. Label Passage 1. It is written in third person, covers telephones across the country over many decades, and gives causes (“The main reasons for the change were cost and speed”). Its purpose is to inform and explain.

Step 2. Label Passage 2. It is told in first person by an operator's child about one town, Alder Creek, and reflects on what the change meant. Its purpose is to narrate and reflect.

Step 3. The choice that pairs an explanation of how and why dial systems replaced switchboards with one family's experience matches both labels. The tempting wrong choice swaps the passages; check each passage's point of view before you choose.
options: Passage 1 argues that dial systems were a mistake, while Passage 2 defends the change to dial telephones.
Passage 1 tells the story of one operator's family, while Passage 2 gives a general history of switchboards.
Passage 1 explains how and why dial systems replaced switchboards; Passage 2 shows how one family lived it.
Passage 1 urges readers to learn about early inventors, while Passage 2 urges readers to support fire crews.
why: This gets both passages wrong. Passage 1 says the dial system “did exactly what it promised,” and the narrator of Passage 2 agrees it was progress but also sees what was lost; she does not simply defend it.
This swaps the passages. The single family's story is Passage 2 (“My mother ran the switchboard”); the general history is Passage 1.
Neither passage urges readers to do anything. Inventors are mentioned once in Passage 1, and the fire in Passage 2 is part of the story, not a call for support.

items.prompt: Which statement best compares the two passages' points of view on the change to dial telephones?
items.hint: Compare the last paragraph of each passage. What does each say the change accomplished, and what else does the narrator notice?
items.explain:
Step 1. Passage 1's view: its last sentence says the dial system “did exactly what it promised: it made calling faster and cheaper for millions of people.” That presents the change as a success.

Step 2. Passage 2's view: the narrator says, “People tell me the dial system was progress, and I agree.” But she also tells about the night a distant operator could not help and ends with “help found the Pruitts because a woman was awake who knew the way.” She accepts the change but sees a loss.

Step 3. The choice that pairs a success story with a narrator who agrees but sees what was lost captures both. The “both present it as a loss” choice ignores that the narrator says, “I agree.”
options: Both passages present the dial system as a loss that should never have happened.
Passage 1 calls it a success; the narrator agrees it was progress yet sees what was lost.
Passage 1 criticizes the telephone company, while the narrator of Passage 2 praises its installers.
Passage 1 is full of personal emotion, while Passage 2 avoids expressing any feelings at all.
why: Passage 1 says the dial system “did exactly what it promised,” and the narrator says, “People tell me the dial system was progress, and I agree.” Neither treats it as a mistake.
Passage 1 reports what telephone companies did without criticism. Passage 2 calls the installers “friendly” but never praises the company.
This reverses the passages. Passage 1 is a neutral history; Passage 2 is full of feeling, such as the mother “counting what had been gained and what had been lost.”

items.prompt: Which statement best compares how the two later-start passages use evidence?
items.hint: List the kinds of evidence in each passage. Then look for any claim in Passage 2 that has no source.
items.explain:
Step 1. List Passage 1's evidence: tardy, sleep-survey, and grade numbers from a district report (paragraph 2); a research finding about teen body clocks and a pediatrician's quote (paragraph 3); the boosters' statement (paragraph 4); and the research director's caution (paragraph 5).

Step 2. List Passage 2's evidence: Harlow's eleven years of coaching and what happened to her players (paragraphs 1–3), two figures taken from the district (the cost and the start times), and claims with no source: “Every athlete I know was more tired this year than last” (an unsupported generalization) and “That money could hire a full-time tutor at every high school” (no source given).

Step 3. The choice that contrasts a district report and several sources with Harlow's experience and some unsourced claims matches both lists. The tempting wrong choice trusts Harlow because she was there every day, but one team's experience cannot show what the survey and records measured across two schools.
options: Passage 1 relies only on statistics from the district's report, while Passage 2 relies only on quotations from sleep doctors.
Both passages rely mainly on the personal stories of students, parents, and coaches rather than on data from the pilot year.
Passage 2 is more reliable than Passage 1 because its writer was at a pilot school every single day of the whole pilot year.
Passage 1 rests on a district report and quotes from several sources; Passage 2 rests on Harlow's experience and unsourced claims.
why: This is wrong twice: Passage 1 also quotes a pediatrician, the boosters, and the research director, and Passage 2 quotes no doctors at all.
Passage 1 is built on data from a district report (tardies, sleep survey, grades). Only Passage 2 leans on personal experience.
This judges evidence by the writer's experience. One coach's view of her own team cannot show what happened to students across two schools; the district's records and survey measured that.

items.skill: Synthesis: how one text relates to another
items.prompt: How does the information in paragraph 5 of Passage 1 relate to Harlow's argument in Passage 2?
items.hint: Reread paragraph 5 sentence by sentence. Which parts would Harlow agree with? Is there any part she would not?
items.explain:
Step 1. Summarize paragraph 5. The director calls the results “encouraging but limited,” says two schools for one year is “a small sample,” and says the district would keep measuring “if the board approves the change districtwide.”

Step 2. Compare with Harlow. She wants a smaller test “so we can see whether the benefits hold up.” The director's caution about limited evidence agrees with her doubt. But he talks about measuring after a districtwide approval, while she asks the board to vote no. So the paragraph partly supports her and partly complicates her argument.

Step 3. The “partly supports” choice describes this mixed relationship. The “fully supports” choice is tempting, but the director never recommends rejecting the plan.
options: It fully supports Harlow, because the director recommends that the board reject the later start for every high school.
It partly supports Harlow: the director calls the evidence limited, but he speaks of measuring a districtwide change, not rejecting it.
It contradicts Harlow, because the director says the later start was clearly the cause of the drop in first-period tardies.
It has no connection to Harlow's argument, because the director discusses only the cost of hiring extra bus drivers.
why: The director never recommends rejecting the plan. He says the district “would want to keep measuring if the board approves the change districtwide.”
The director makes no claim about causes. He says the results are “encouraging but limited” and the sample is small.
Paragraph 5 does not mention bus costs. It is about how much the pilot results can prove.

items.skill: Synthesis: how one text complicates another
items.prompt: How does the event described in paragraph 3 of Passage 2 complicate a claim made in Passage 1?
items.hint: First, summarize what happens in paragraph 3 of Passage 2. Then find the sentence in Passage 1 about emergencies.
items.explain:
Step 1. Summarize paragraph 3 of Passage 2: Mrs. Pruitt dialed “0,” but the operator, sixty miles away, needed a street address the Pruitts did not have. The local former operator, who knew the way, got help.

Step 2. Find the related claim in Passage 1. Paragraph 4 says that “for emergencies and special requests, callers could still dial ‘0’ to reach an operator.”

Step 3. The story shows a case where reaching a distant operator was not enough. It does not prove Passage 1 wrong in general, but it shows the claim is not the whole story. That is what complicate means. The tempting wrong choice says the call never went through, but the passage says an operator answered.
options: Passage 1 says operators knew the people on their lines, but Passage 2 shows the narrator's mother did not know the Pruitts.
Passage 1 says small exchanges were among the last to change, but Passage 2 shows Alder Creek was the first town converted.
Passage 1 says callers could still dial “0” in emergencies, but in Passage 2 the distant operator needed an address the Pruitts lacked.
Passage 1 says dial systems connected calls in seconds, but in Passage 2 Mrs. Pruitt's call to “0” never went through to anyone.
why: The mother clearly knew the Pruitts: Mrs. Pruitt called her house, and she reached the fire chief and three neighbors “all by memory.” Passage 2 says she knew every family on the board.
Passage 2 never says Alder Creek was the first town converted. It gives no comparison with other towns at all.
The call did go through: “The operator who answered was in an office sixty miles away.” The problem was what she did not know, not a failed connection.

items.prompt:
Complete each statement about the two telephone passages.

Paragraph 4 of Passage 1 says that for emergencies, callers could still dial “0” to reach an operator. The fire in paragraph 3 of Passage 2 {{0}} that claim.

Both passages show that {{1}}.

Passage 2 {{2}} Passage 1 by showing what the change meant to one operator's family.
items.hint: For each blank, use ADAC. For the middle blank, use the two-check rule: find a line in each passage.
items.explain:
Blank 1. Passage 1 says callers could still dial “0” for emergencies. In Passage 2, Mrs. Pruitt did exactly that, but the distant operator needed a street address the Pruitts did not have. The claim is still partly true (an operator answered), but it is not the whole story: the fire complicates it.

Blank 2. Passage 1, paragraph 2: operators “passed along messages, told callers where a doctor could be found, and sounded the alarm when there was a fire.” Passage 2: the mother kept a notebook of who was sick or traveling and called the fire chief and neighbors from memory. Both show small-town operators often did more than connect calls. The 1890s inventors appear only in Passage 1.

Blank 3. The memoir gives an inside view of a change that Passage 1 describes from the outside. It adds to Passage 1 without disagreeing with it.

options: complicates
proves
repeats
has nothing to do with
why: The fire shows a case where reaching a distant operator did not get help to the Pruitts, so it cannot prove the claim. It shows the claim is not the whole story.
Passage 2 does not restate the claim; it describes a night when dialing “0” was not enough, which pushes against the claim.
The fire is about an emergency call to “0,” which is exactly what Passage 1's claim is about.

options: small-town operators often did more than connect calls
dial systems made telephone calls slower
the old switchboards should be brought back
inventors built automatic switches in the 1890s
why: Both passages say the opposite: Passage 1 says calls went through in seconds, and the narrator says, “Calls are faster.”
Neither passage says this. Passage 1 calls the change a success, and the narrator says she agrees it was progress.
Only Passage 1 mentions the 1890s inventors. Passage 2 never does, so this fails the two-check rule.

options: adds to
disagrees with
summarizes
corrects
why: The narrator agrees the dial system was progress, so Passage 2 does not take the opposite side. Its family story is new information that fits the history.
A summary would restate Passage 1's main points. Passage 2 tells a new, personal story that Passage 1 never includes.
Passage 2 does not say Passage 1 got its facts wrong. One family's experience adds a personal side to the history.

items.prompt: Select two ideas that both the author of Passage 1 and the narrator of Passage 2 would accept.
items.hint: An idea counts only if you can point to support for it in Passage 1 and in Passage 2.
items.explain:
Use the two-check rule on each idea.

  • Faster calls: Passage 1 says, “Calls went through in seconds,” and that the system made calling “faster and cheaper.” The narrator says, “Calls are faster.” Both.
  • Operators knew the people they served: Passage 1 says operators helped “because they knew the people on their lines.” Passage 2 says the mother “knew every family on the board by their ring.” Both.

The idea that dial systems removed any need for an operator is the most tempting wrong choice, but Passage 1 itself says callers could still reach an operator, and the fire in Passage 2 shows a person was needed.
options: The dial system made telephone calls faster.
Small-town operators knew the people they served.
Dial systems removed any need for a human operator.
Switchboard work was dull and took no real skill.
The company should have kept the Alder Creek board.
why: Passage 1 says callers could still dial “0” to reach an operator, and in Passage 2 a person who knew the way was needed the night of the fire.
Passage 1 lists skilled work beyond connecting calls, such as passing messages and sounding fire alarms, and Passage 2 shows the mother handling an emergency from memory. Neither calls the work dull.
The narrator says, “People tell me the dial system was progress, and I agree.” Neither writer argues for keeping the old board.

stimuli.title: Paired Passages: Dining at the Curb
stimuli.html:
Passage 1: Main Street Dining Pilot Wraps Up First Summer

(1) For five months this year, the city of Bellport turned 14 parking spaces on Main Street into “parklets,” small outdoor dining areas built on platforms at the curb. The pilot ran from May through September and cost the city about $96,000 for platforms, railings, and planters.

(2) According to city sales-tax records, restaurant sales on the four blocks with parklets were 18 percent higher than during the same months last year. Sales at other Main Street stores were about the same as last year. A parking study found that the share of occupied spaces on nearby blocks rose from 71 percent to 84 percent at lunchtime; planners consider a block full at 90 percent.

(3) “People told us the street felt alive for the first time in years,” said planning director Owen Pratt. Pratt cautioned that one summer of data is not enough to decide the program's future, since a new hotel also opened downtown in June. The city council will decide this winter whether to bring the parklets back next year.

Passage 2: Parklets Are Great for Restaurants. What About the Rest of Us?

by Gloria Benton, owner, Benton Hardware

(1) My family has run Benton Hardware on Main Street for thirty-one years. I'm glad the restaurants had a good summer; I ate at the parklet outside Rosa's more than once. But before the council brings the parklets back, it should hear from the businesses that lost the curb.

(2) My customers buy bags of concrete, ladders, and paint by the gallon. They need to park near my door. This summer, the two spaces in front of my store were a dining area. A contractor who has shopped with us for years told me he started driving to the big-box store on Route 40 because he could never find a spot.

(3) Half of my regular customers have stopped coming downtown since the parklets went in. The city's parking study says nearby blocks still had open spaces, but a space three blocks away does not help someone carrying forty pounds of concrete.

(4) I am not asking the council to end the program. I am asking it to keep parklets in front of restaurants and to turn the spaces in front of stores like mine into short-term loading spaces.
stimuli.source: Both passages were written for this course.

stimuli.title: Paired Passages: Paying the Fare by Phone
stimuli.html:
Passage 1: Transit Agency Reports on Mobile Fare Pilot

(1) Last spring, the Carson Valley Transit Agency began letting riders on three bus routes pay their fares with a phone app instead of paper passes. Riders scan a code on their phone as they board. Paper passes are still sold at three locations: the downtown transit center, the public library, and the county services building.

(2) In its six-month report, the agency said that 62 percent of riders on the three routes were using the app by the end of the pilot. Average boarding time at busy stops fell from 41 seconds to 29 seconds, which helped buses stay closer to schedule. The agency estimates that expanding the app to all 14 routes would save about $210,000 a year in printing and sales costs.

(3) “Riders tell us the app is faster and that they like not having to find a place that sells passes,” said agency spokesperson Mia Torres. Torres noted that the pilot routes serve mostly commuters and students, who may be more likely to own smartphones than other riders. The agency board will vote next month on whether to expand the app and reduce the number of places that sell paper passes.

Passage 2: Don't Leave Riders Without Phones Behind

by Harold Greene, director, Eastside Senior Center

(1) I have run the Eastside Senior Center for fifteen years, and every week I watch our members ride the bus to doctor visits and the grocery store. I don't doubt that the app has made boarding faster; anyone who has waited behind someone counting coins knows how slow paper can be. But before the board cuts back on paper passes, it should think about who gets left out.

(2) Many of our members do not own smartphones, and some who do cannot read the small print on the screen. Last month, one of our members, an 81-year-old retired nurse, rode two buses to the transit center to buy a pass, only to find the line out the door.

(3) Most of our members will simply stop riding if paper passes become hard to buy. Then they will miss appointments and end up in the hospital, which costs everyone more.

(4) I am not asking the board to scrap the app. I am asking it to keep selling paper passes at grocery stores and senior centers, where older riders already go.
stimuli.source: Both passages were written for this course.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes how the purposes of the two passages differ?
items.explain: Passage 1 is a news report: costs, sales figures, a parking study, and an official's comments, with no request. Its purpose is to inform. Passage 2 is a letter from a store owner that ends with a request: “keep parklets in front of restaurants and… turn the spaces in front of stores like mine into short-term loading spaces.” Its purpose is to persuade the council to change the program. The tempting wrong choice says both want the program ended, but Benton rules that out herself.
options: Passage 1 reports the results of the parklet pilot; Passage 2 urges the council to change the program.
