Passage 1 urges the council to bring the parklets back next year; Passage 2 reports the pilot's results.
Both passages try to convince the city council to end the parklet program before next summer begins.
Passage 1 tells the story of one restaurant's summer; Passage 2 explains how the parking study worked.
why: This swaps the passages. Passage 1 reports numbers and quotes and never says what the council should do; it is Passage 2 that makes a request.
Passage 1 takes no position, and Benton says directly, “I am not asking the council to end the program.”
Passage 1 covers the whole pilot, not one restaurant, and Passage 2 mentions the parking study only to question what it shows.

items.prompt: Which statement best compares the points of view of the two passages?
items.explain: Passage 1 is a third-person report. Its only opinions belong to the person it quotes, Owen Pratt, and the writer never takes a side. Passage 2 is first person from Gloria Benton, an insider with a stake: the spaces in front of her store were taken. She accepts that the program helped restaurants but asks for a change. The most tempting wrong choice treats Pratt's quote as the writer's own opinion.
options: Passage 1 reports from outside the debate; Passage 2 speaks as an affected owner who wants the program changed.
Both writers oppose the parklet program and want the council to end it for good before next summer begins on Main Street.
Passage 1 is written by a restaurant owner who gained from the pilot; Passage 2 is written by a city planner.
Passage 1 strongly supports the parklets in its own voice; Passage 2 is a neutral report that takes no side.
why: Passage 1 takes no side, and Benton is glad the restaurants did well and says she is “not asking the council to end the program.”
Passage 1 is a third-person report that quotes the planning director; it is not written by a restaurant owner. Passage 2 is by a hardware store owner.
The praise in Passage 1 (“the street felt alive”) is inside quotation marks and credited to Pratt. Reporting a view is not holding it. Passage 2 is first person and makes a request.

items.prompt: The sentences below are from Passage 2. Click the sentence in which Benton concedes a point that helps supporters of the parklets.
items.explain: A concession admits something that helps the other side. Benton says she is “glad the restaurants had a good summer” and even ate at a parklet. The restaurants' success is the strongest point in favor of the program, so admitting it is a concession. The next sentence turns with “But” to her own point. The first sentence gives her background, and the last two are her evidence.
spans: My family has run Benton Hardware on Main Street for thirty-one years.
I'm glad the restaurants had a good summer; I ate at the parklet outside Rosa's more than once.
But before the council brings the parklets back, it should hear from the businesses that lost the curb.
My customers buy bags of concrete, ladders, and paint by the gallon.
They need to park near my door.
items.why: Some students click the sentence that begins with “But.” That sentence is the turn back to Benton's own argument. The concession comes just before it: she admits the restaurants did well.

items.prompt: Which statement is supported by both passages?
items.explain: Run the two-check rule. Passage 1: restaurant sales on the parklet blocks were “18 percent higher.” Passage 2: “I'm glad the restaurants had a good summer.” Both support restaurants did well. The “main reason” choice is tempting because sales rose during the pilot, but Pratt points to the new hotel as another possible cause.
options: Restaurants on Main Street did well during the parklet pilot.
Half of Main Street's regular shoppers stopped coming downtown.
The parklets were the main reason that restaurant sales went up.
The blocks near the parklets were completely full at lunchtime.
why: Only Benton says this, and only about her own customers. Passage 1 reports that sales at other Main Street stores held steady. It fails the two-check rule.
Neither passage says this. Pratt warns that a new hotel also opened in June, and Benton never says what caused the sales increase.
Both passages say the opposite: Passage 1 reports 84 percent occupancy, below the 90 percent “full” mark, and Benton says the study found open spaces nearby.

items.prompt: Select two details from Passage 1 that Benton does not mention in Passage 2.
items.explain: Search Passage 2 for each detail. The open spaces, the lost parking spaces, and the council's decision all appear in Benton's letter. Two details do not: that sales at other Main Street stores held steady, and that a new hotel opened in June. Notice that both are details that weaken Benton's case or the case that parklets alone drove sales; writers arguing one side often leave out facts like these.
options: Sales at other Main Street stores were about the same as last year.
A new hotel opened downtown in June.
Nearby blocks still had open parking spaces.
The parklets took over parking spaces on Main Street.

vocab.def: Two texts on the same topic that are read together and compared.
vocab.example: A news article about a new law and a letter from a citizen who opposes it.

vocab.def: To combine information from two or more sources to form a new, fuller understanding.
vocab.example: Using both a report and a worker's letter to explain how a policy affects different people.

vocab.def: The main point an author wants the reader to accept as true.
vocab.example: The city should spend money on speed humps instead of new signs.

vocab.def: The reason an author writes a text, such as to inform, explain, persuade, or tell a story.
vocab.example: A fact sheet informs; an editorial persuades.

vocab.def: Who is speaking in a text and how that person sees the topic, including beliefs and personal stake.
vocab.example: A first-person memoir by a lighthouse keeper's daughter.

vocab.def: Facts, data, examples, quotations, or experiences an author uses to support a claim.
vocab.example: Reported crashes fell from 41 to 27 during the pilot year.

vocab.def: A short personal story used as an example. It can illustrate a point but cannot prove that something is true for everyone.
vocab.example: My neighbor kept a library book for six months.

vocab.def: A broad statement about a whole group. It is unsupported when the author gives no evidence that it is true for the group.
vocab.example: Everyone knows drivers ignore speed limit signs.

vocab.def: A point where an author admits that the other side is right about something.
vocab.example: I'll admit that crashes on the pilot streets went down.

vocab.def: To support or confirm information from another source.
vocab.example: The second article corroborates the first by reporting the same cost.

vocab.def: To state the opposite of, or to show that something is not true.
vocab.example: The library's data contradicts the claim that returns would fall.

vocab.def: To show that a point is not the whole story by adding a limit, exception, or cost.
vocab.example: The supervisor's letter complicates the report by noting that loading-dock jobs don't fit a four-day schedule.

vocab.def: A leaning toward one side that can shape what a writer includes or leaves out.
vocab.example: A company's announcement may highlight only its successes.

vocab.def: A kind of text, such as a news report, letter to the editor, fact sheet, or memoir. The genre is a strong clue to the author's purpose.
vocab.example: A county fact sheet usually informs; a letter to the editor usually persuades.

vocab.def: For a question about what both passages support, you must find support in Passage 1 and in Passage 2. A choice found in only one passage is wrong.
vocab.example: “Crashes went down” appears in the news report and in the driver's letter, so both passages support it.

notes:
Week 6 RLA Study Sheet: Comparing Two Texts

The routine

  1. Read P1 alone. Label: who, main point, purpose.
  2. Read P2 alone. Label it the same way.
  3. Compare on four points (chart below).
  4. Synthesize with ADAC.
  5. Answer, using the two-check rule for “both” questions.

Purpose and genre clues

  • Inform: news report, fact sheet, textbook
  • Explain: how-to, science or history article
  • Persuade: editorial, letter, speech; strong words, call to action
  • Narrate or reflect: memoir, diary, story; “I,” feelings, scenes

ADAC: how texts relate

  • Agree: both support the same point
  • Disagree: opposite claims
  • Add: new information that fits
  • Complicate: a limit, exception, or cost

Point of view questions

  • Who is speaking? First or third person?
  • Insider or outsider?
  • What does the speaker believe?
  • What is at stake for the speaker?
  • Reporting a view is not holding it.

Comparison chart

PointPassage 1Passage 2
Claim or central idea
Purpose
Point of view
Evidence (type and strength)

Judging evidence

StrongerWeaker
Specific data with a named source“Everyone knows,” “always,” “nobody”
Quotes from people who work in the fieldOne anecdote used to prove something about everyone
Typical, relevant examplesNumbers or predictions with no source

Paired-passage questions

  • “Supported by both”: two-check rule. Find a line in Passage 1 and a line in Passage 2.
  • “In one passage but not the other”: find it in one, then search the other to rule it out.
  • “How does Passage 2 relate to Passage 1?”: name the ADAC relationship first, then match. Many pairs agree on facts and complicate conclusions.

Traps: giving one author the other's idea; a choice true for only one passage; assuming opposing writers disagree about everything; treating a reporter's quote as the reporter's opinion.
